entities.name: Tar-Amandil
entities.short_description: Tar-Amandil was the third King of Númenor.
entities.description:
Tar-Amandil was the third King of Númenor.

Tar-Amandil was actually Númenor's second ruler; his father, Vardamir Nólimon, had declined to take the throne upon the death of his own father, Elros Tar-Minyatur. He abdicated due to advanced age in favor of his son Tar-Amandil but was still by right of succession the ruler, and Vardamir is still counted in the list of kings, making him the second king. Thus, Tar-Amandil was listed as the third King of Númenor. As Vardamir was potentially Half-elven like Elros, Tar-Amandil may have been a Half-elf of the third generation, giving him a slow maturity and long youth like the Elves, while being fated for mortality like Men. He had three children: Tar-Elendil, his eldest son who would succeed him, Eärendur, and a daughter named Mairen.

Tar-Amandil surrendered the Sceptre of Númenor in SA 590 and was succeeded by Tar-Elendil. He died in the year 603 of the Second Age at the age of 411.

Amandil is a Quenya name that meant either "Friend of Aman" or "Devoted to Aman", from Aman and (n)dil ("friend").

entities.name: Telemnar
entities.short_description: Telemnar was the twenty-sixth King of Gondor.
entities.description:
Telemnar was the twenty-sixth King of Gondor.

Telemnar became King after his father, Minardil, died in an attack by the Corsairs of Umbar at Pelargir in TA 1634. Due to this renewed threat from the Corsairs, he immediately began building up Gondor's fleets to defeat them; but was forced to stop when the Great Plague struck. This plague ravaged Gondor and many died; especially in Osgiliath and Minas Ithil. During the plague, both Telemnar and his children died. The White Tree also withered and died during this time. He was succeeded by his nephew Tarondor, the son of Telemnar's younger brother Minastan.

His father's reign was brief but his own reign was even briefer. He was the shortest reigning King of Gondor.

The name Telemnar was a Quenya word that was likely to have come from the words telempë, meaning "silver", and nár, meaning "flame". This would give the meaning "silver flame" to his name.

entities.name: Tar-Minastir
entities.short_description: Tar-Minastir was the eleventh King of Númenor. He was king during the War of the Elves and Sauron in the mid-Second Age, he helped defeat Sauron by sending a relief force to the aid of Gil-galad who was under siege in…
entities.description:
Tar-Minastir was the eleventh King of Númenor. He was king during the War of the Elves and Sauron in the mid-Second Age, he helped defeat Sauron by sending a relief force to the aid of Gil-galad who was under siege in Middle-earth.

Tar-Minastir was the son of Isilmo and succeeded his aunt, Queen Tar-Telperiën, when she died. He was the grandson of King Tar-Súrion. His heart yearned for the west as did many in his time and loved the Elves but envied them. At some point during his rule, he had a great tower built on Oromet so that he could gaze upon the west and dream.

During his rule, Sauron invaded Eriador from Calenardhon in SA 1695 and the realm of Eregion fell. Sauron advanced to Lindon and Rivendell. In SA 1700, Tar-Minastir sent a naval force under the command of Ciryatur to save Lindon. Ciryatur's forces drove Sauron's army back from the Grey Havens and then pursued him to Tharbad, where further Númenórean forces helped defeat Sauron at the Battle of the Gwathló. Battered but not utterly defeated Sauron retreated back to Mordor in SA 1701 swearing revenge.

From Tar-Minastir's reign, the Númenóreans began establishing permanent settlements in Middle-earth.

entities.name: Tar-Atanamir
entities.short_description: Tar-Atanamir also known as Atanamir the Great was the thirteenth King of Númenor.
entities.description:
Tar-Atanamir also known as Atanamir the Great was the thirteenth King of Númenor.

Tar-Atanamir succeeded his father, King Tar-Ciryatan, in SA 2029. He was married to an unnamed woman and had a son named Tar-Ancalimon and another unnamed child that eventually led up to Herucalmo. Tar-Atanamir began to speak against the Valar in particular the Ban of the Valar and the Gift of Ilúvatar. He was also the first king who was unwilling to give up his throne voluntarily before his death, and to let himself die while he was still strong in mind and body. His reign is thus generally considered to constitute the beginning of Númenor's moral decline.

The Valar were perturbed that the Númenóreans spoke against the Ban of the Valar and sent ambassadors to Tar-Atanamir to attempt to reassure them and halt their growing fear of death. The king demanded to know why his ancestors Eärendil and Tuor lived in Valinor and had eternal life yet he did not. The ambassadors answered that theirs was a fate apart and that the Undying Lands did not themselves make their inhabitants immortal, but were named for those that dwelled in them. Tar-Atanamir was not satisfied with these answers.

He was the first king to refuse to die willingly and give up the Sceptre; death instead took him by force and thus his reign ended. Thus every ruler afterwards did not renounce their reign and accept death before dotage. Tar-Atanamir ruled for one hundred ninety-two years and was succeeded by his son, Tar-Ancalimon. After his death the lifespans of the House of Elros would begin to wane.

entities.name: Tar-Ciryatan
entities.short_description: Tar-Ciryatan, or Ar-Balkumagân in Adûnaic, was the twelfth King of Númenor. His rule marked the first coming of the shadow upon the Númenóreans and their rulers; the speaking out openly against the Valar and the Ban,…
entities.description:
Tar-Ciryatan, or Ar-Balkumagân in Adûnaic, was the twelfth King of Númenor. His rule marked the first coming of the shadow upon the Númenóreans and their rulers; the speaking out openly against the Valar and the Ban, colonialism, and dominion abroad.

Tar-Ciryatan was born in SA 1634 and was the son of Tar-Minastir. He loved ships and everything connected to ship-lore and ship building. His heart was restless in Númenor and before succeeding his father, he went on many voyages around the world travelling east, north, and south but never west as many yearned to do but never could because of the Ban of the Valar.

He succeeded his father in SA 1869, wresting the Sceptre from him prematurely. Tar-Ciryatan became a mighty king, building great armadas of ships, and the Númenóreans began large-scale colonization of the coasts of Middle-earth, holding the Middle Men in subjugation and demanding great tribute from them. As Tar-Ciryatan was greedy of wealth in these days, he received the pick of the many metals and gems that had been taken by his men in payment or as spoils of war.

He abdicated in SA 2029 after ruling for one-hundred and sixty years, and was succeeded by his son, Tar-Atanamir. He died in SA 2035.

entities.name: Tar-Anárion
entities.short_description: Tar-Anárion was the eighth King of Númenor.
entities.description:
Tar-Anárion was the eighth King of Númenor.

Tar-Anárion succeeded his mother, Tar-Ancalimë in SA 1280. Little is known about Tar-Anárion's rule. His two eldest children were female, but both declined the throne for uncertain reasons, and they disliked and feared Ancalimë, who refused to let them marry. Therefore, he was succeeded by his son, Tar-Súrion.

Anárion means "Sun-son" or "Child of the Sun" from the Quenya anar ("sun") and -ion ("son, descendant of").

entities.name: Thuringwethil
entities.short_description: Thuringwethil was a vampire of Sauron at Tol-in-Gaurhoth, during the First Age.
entities.description:
Thuringwethil was a vampire of Sauron at Tol-in-Gaurhoth, during the First Age.

The origins of Thuringwethil are untold. Her ability to change form suggests that she may have been an Ainu or a skin-changer.

Sometime before the Quest for the Silmaril, Thuringwethil became the messenger of Sauron at Tol-in-Gaurhoth, formerly Tol Sirion, often flying to Angband in the curséd

In the year 466, Lúthien disguised herself in Thuringwethil's vile

entities.name: Tar-Vanimeldë
entities.short_description: Tar-Vanimeldë was the sixteenth ruler of Númenor and third and last ruling Queen of Númenor.
entities.description:
Tar-Vanimeldë was the sixteenth ruler of Númenor and third and last ruling Queen of Númenor.

Tar-Vanimeldë was the daughter and heir of Tar-Telemmaitë. She had little interest in ruling, loving rather culture and the arts such as music and dance, however, and left the day-to-day chores of monarchy to her husband, the nobleman Herucalmo.

Tar-Vanimeldë ruled for 111 years. When she died in SA 2637 at the age of 360 years, the Kingship should have gone to her son, Tar-Alcarin, but Herucalmo usurped the throne and ruled for twenty years as King Tar-Anducal. His rule was not considered legitimate, and in the official records Vanimeldë was directly followed by Alcarin.

The name Vanimeldë means "Beautiful Beloved" from the Quenya vanima ("beautiful, fair")

entities.name: Tarondor of Arnor
entities.short_description: Tarondor was the seventh High King of Arnor.
entities.description:
Tarondor was the seventh High King of Arnor.

Tarondor was born in TA 372 to Tarcil and his unnamed wife. He ascended to the throne of Arnor in TA 515 on the death of his father Tarcil. Little is recorded of his reign. He died in TA 602 after an eighty-seven year rule, and was succeeded by his son Valandur.

The name Tarondor was a Quenya word that meant 'Royal Rock'.

entities.name: Tarcil
entities.short_description: Tarcil was the sixth High King of Arnor.
entities.description:
Tarcil was the sixth High King of Arnor.

Tarcil was born in TA 280 to Arantar and his unnamed wife. He ascended the throne of Arnor in TA 435 on the death of his father. His reign was without event for eighty years and he died in TA 515 and was succeeded by his son Tarondor. He was two-hundred and thirty-five years of age.

The name Tarcil (also spelt Tarkil) means "High Man", a synonym for Dúnadan, in Quenya. In The History of The Lord of the Rings it appears as another nickname for Aragorn. The Orcish term "tark" for a Dúnadan is without doubt derived from this.

entities.name: Tar-Telperiën
entities.short_description: Tar-Telperiën was the tenth ruler and second Ruling Queen of Númenor. She succeeded her father King Tar-Súrion.
entities.description:
Tar-Telperiën was the tenth ruler and second Ruling Queen of Númenor. She succeeded her father King Tar-Súrion.

Tar-Telperiën ruled for 175 years. During her reign, the Rings of Power were forged, and Sauron conquered Eriador. She did little to react to these events. She refused to marry and bore no children. She was succeeded by Tar-Minastir, the son of her younger brother, Isilmo. She died in the year SA 1731 at the age of 411.

The name Telperiën might be related to the Quenya tyelpë ("silver") and -ien, a feminine suffix.

She was most likely named after Telperion, the White Tree of Valinor.

entities.name: Telchar
entities.short_description: Telchar was a Dwarf of Nogrod in the Blue Mountains during the First Age.
entities.description:
Telchar was a Dwarf of Nogrod in the Blue Mountains during the First Age.

Telchar was one of the greatest smiths of the First Age of Middle-earth, having learned from Gamil Zirak the old. Telchar was commonly regarded amongst the greatest smiths of all time, save only Fëanor and Celebrimbor. Among his works were the knife Angrist, the sword Narsil (later reforged as Andúril), and the Dragon-helm of Dor-lómin, worn eventually by Túrin Turambar.

Neither Telchar's lifespan nor details of his personal life are known, but it is known that the Dragon Helm of Dor-lómin was made shortly after the dragon Glaurung first appeared, in the 265th year of the First Age.

In earlier versions of the legendarium, such as the second version of The Lay of the Children of Húrin (in The Lays of Beleriand) and those in the The Shaping of Middle-earth, Telchar was originally one of the Dwarves of Belegost. In this version Telchar made the Dragon-helm in the dark dwarf-land in the deeps of time.
entities.image_credit: Fair-use identification thumbnail via Fandom. Character / franchise art © Tolkien Estate / New Line / Warner Bros. / Amazon (as applicable). Not free or redistributable artwork.

entities.name: Thorondir
entities.short_description: Thorondir was the 22nd Ruling Steward of Gondor.
entities.description:
Thorondir was the 22nd Ruling Steward of Gondor.

Thorondir was born in TA 2782 and was the son of Belecthor II. When Belecthor passed away in TA 2872, the White Tree of Gondor also withered and died. Thorondir succeeded his father as the 22nd Ruling Steward and decided to leave the dead tree standing until the King returned, as no seedling could be found.

Thorondir died in TA 2882 at the age of 100 after 10 years of rule, and was succeeded by his son Túrin II.

Although the name Thorondir has no given meaning, it consists of the Sindarin thor(on) ("eagle").

entities.name: Telumehtar
entities.short_description: Telumehtar, also known as Telumehtar Umbardacil, was the twenty-eighth King of Gondor. He is most famous for his victory over the Corsairs of Umbar in TA 1810.
entities.description:
Telumehtar, also known as Telumehtar Umbardacil, was the twenty-eighth King of Gondor. He is most famous for his victory over the Corsairs of Umbar in TA 1810.

Telumehtar succeeded his father Tarondor as King in TA 1798. Early in his reign, the Corsairs of Umbar raided the coasts of Gondor and terrorized shipping in the Bay of Belfalas. King Telemnar had been preparing an expedition to avenge the death of his father Minardil, but the outbreak of the Great Plague sapped Gondor's strength. 174 years later, Telumehtar resolved to end the war and gain vengeance, so he assembled a large force in TA 1810 and recaptured the city of Umbar. After this event he took the title Umbardacil, meaning "Victor over Umbar". In this war, the Corsairs suffered total defeat and the descendants of Castamir the Usurper all perished. Umbar was for a time held again by Gondor.

Telumehtar ruled for fifty-two years. He had two sons: his eldest, Narmacil II (who succeeded him in TA 1850), and his younger son Arciryas.

entities.name: Tindómiel
entities.short_description: Tindómiel was the second child and only daughter of Elros Tar-Minyatur, Half-elf and the first King of Númenor.
entities.description:
Tindómiel was the second child and only daughter of Elros Tar-Minyatur, Half-elf and the first King of Númenor.

She was born after SA 61 and was the sister of Manwendil, Atanalcar, and the short reigning King Vardamir Nólimon. Nothing else is known of her life or whether she married and had children.

In The Nature of Middle-earth J.R.R. Tolkien considered making the children of Elros Half-elves, gaining the same choice of mortality as the children of Elrond. Whether he adopted this idea fully is unclear.

The name Tindómiel means "Morning Star" from the Quenya tindome ("twilight of dawn") and el ("star"). It may also mean "Daughter of Twilight" from the feminine suffix -iel.

entities.name: Oromë
entities.short_description: Oromë (Quenya: "Horn-blower"), also known as Aldaron (Quenya: "Lord of Forests"), Araw (Sindarin), and Arǭmēz, was an Ainu, one of the Aratar and the Vala responsible for the hunt. He was the brother of Nessa and…
entities.description:
Oromë (Quenya: "Horn-blower"), also known as Aldaron (Quenya: "Lord of Forests"), Araw (Sindarin), and Arǭmēz, was an Ainu, one of the Aratar and the Vala responsible for the hunt. He was the brother of Nessa and husband of Vána.

During the Years of the Trees, after most of the Valar had withdrawn completely from Middle-earth and hidden themselves in Aman, Oromë still hunted in the forests of Middle-earth on occasion. Thus, it was he who discovered the Elves when they first awoke at Cuiviénen and named them the Eldar. Thereafter, he remained close in friendship with them.

A powerful huntsman, he was active in the struggles against Morgoth. He had a great horn called the Valaróma and a great steed named Nahar.

In legend, Oromë is said to have first created the Rainbow or "Bridge of Heaven" using golden threads of Vána's hair, during the Hiding of Valinor.
entities.image_credit: Fair-use identification thumbnail via Fandom. Character / franchise art © Tolkien Estate / New Line / Warner Bros. / Amazon (as applicable). Not free or redistributable artwork.

entities.name: Rúmil
entities.short_description: Philology, the study of comparative and historical linguistics, especially of the medieval period, had a major influence on J. R. R. Tolkien's fantasy world of Middle-earth. He was a professional philologist, and made…
entities.description:
Rúmil was a knowledgeable loremaster of the Ñoldor living in the city of Tirion, in Valinor.

Rúmil was possibly born in Valinor, or was perhaps one of the firstborn Elves. He thrived in Valinor, being the first to invent the art of writing down words with pen or brush on many different mediums: he invented the alphabet called Sarati (each letter being a Sarat). This alphabet was later expanded and perfected by Fëanor as the Tengwar. Rúmil was also a skilled linguist, and when the Teleri finally arrived in Valinor he was first to discover just how the Telerin language had changed from Common Eldarin compared to Quenya. He became part of an Elvish culture of loremasters known as the Lambeñgolmor.

When the Ñoldor determined to return to Middle-earth in pursuit of Morgoth, Rúmil was among those who refused the summons of Fëanor, remaining in Tirion as one of the Ñoldor of Finarfin.

Rúmil is a Quenya word. Its origin is not clear - it is possibly derived from rum, meaning 'a secret'.

entities.name: Salmar
entities.short_description: Salmar was a Maia, creator of the Ulumúri. Made for his lord the Vala Ulmo, the Ulumúri were great who produced the music of the Sea. That he was a Maia is confirmed only in the index of .
entities.description:
Salmar was a Maia, creator of the Ulumúri. Made for his lord the Vala Ulmo, the Ulumúri were great who produced the music of the Sea. That he was a Maia is confirmed only in the index of .

Salmar is a Quenya name of unspecified meaning. It was possibly derived from the Quenya word salma, meaning "lyre".

In earlier versions of the legendarium discussed in , Salmar is often identified by the title Noldorin (sometimes "Lirillo" or "Golthadriel" in Gnomish, later Sindarin). He was envisioned as a Vala in the service of Aulë.

entities.name: Olwë
entities.short_description: Olwë was an Elf of the Teleri of Aman. When he and his kin reached Aman, they chose to remain there in both Tol Eressëa and Alqualondë, apart from the rest of the Elves of Aman. Olwë became Lord of Alqualondë and King…
entities.description:
Olwë was an Elf of the Teleri of Aman. When he and his kin reached Aman, they chose to remain there in both Tol Eressëa and Alqualondë, apart from the rest of the Elves of Aman. Olwë became Lord of Alqualondë and King of the Teleri.

He was the father of Eärwen and several unnamed sons. He was the younger brother of Elwë (Elu Thingol) and the older brother of Elmo. Other Telerin Elves such as Nowë (Círdan) were said to be akin to Olwë.

Olwë and both his brothers ware born in Cuiviénen during the Years of the Trees to unnamed parents, and their father was the direct descendant of Enel and Enelyë. After Oromë discovered the Quendi, Elwë and Olwë became both lords of the third clan of the Elves, the later Teleri, and together they lead their people from Cuiviénen to the West. However, during a long wait in Beleriand Elwë disappeared. After years of searching, Olwë grew impatient, and led the greater part of the Teleri to Valinor, on the insistence of the Vala Ulmo.

Olwë became Lord of the island of Tol Eressëa, where the Teleri built a great number of cities, and grew in number. When they finally came to Eldamar some centuries later, Olwë became Lord of Alqualondë. His daughter Eärwen married Finarfin son of Finwë and later High King of the Ñoldor in Valinor, and thus their children, when these returned to Middle-earth, could claim kinship to Thingol, for Eärwen had several sons.

entities.name: Oropher
entities.short_description: Oropher was the Sindar King of the Silvan Elves of Greenwood the Great during the Second Age. He was the father of Thranduil, who would succeed him, and grandfather of Legolas.
entities.description:
Oropher was the Sindar King of the Silvan Elves of Greenwood the Great during the Second Age. He was the father of Thranduil, who would succeed him, and grandfather of Legolas.

Oropher was one of the Sindar of Doriath. After the War of Wrath, he declined to depart Middle-earth as many others did, and instead went over the Blue Mountains with his household. He eventually ended up in Greenwood the Great, where Silvan Elves of Nandorin descent lived, and he was taken by them as lord. His capital was at Amon Lanc.

West of Oropher's realm was the realm of Lórinand across the Anduin, where Amdír, another Sindar, ruled over Silvan Elves.

Before the War of the Last Alliance, Oropher and his folk left their capital at Amon Lanc and crossed Anduin to live with their kin in Lórinand. Three times, he moved his people northwards, eventually settling around Emyn Duir, the Mountains of Mirkwood. His retreat northwards was because of his desire to move "out of range" from the Dwarves of Khazad-dûm and avoid the threat of Mordor.

entities.name: Rómendacil II
entities.short_description: Rómendacil II was the son of King Calmacil, and the elder brother of Calimehtar. He was originally named Minalcar.
entities.description:
Rómendacil II was the son of King Calmacil, and the elder brother of Calimehtar. He was originally named Minalcar.

Minalcar was born in TA 1126, toward the end of the long reign of Hyarmendacil I and he rose to power early because his uncle Narmacil I (eldest son of Atanatar II) wished to devote himself to a life of pleasure.

He was "Regent of the realm" of Gondor from TA 1240 and struck a decisive blow against the Easterlings, whom he heavily defeated in TA 1248 near the Sea of Rhûn. He also fortified Gondor and made pacts with the Northmen of Rhovanion, all before he took the throne. After Narmacil's death, he remained Regent for ten years under his father Calmacil.

When he finally ascended to the throne after the death of his father, he immediately took the name Rómendacil (East-victor), as his distant forefather Tarostar had done. He was responsible for the Argonath, the pillars of the Kings. They stood above Nen Hithoel on the Anduin river long into the Fourth Age and appear prominently in .

entities.name: Siriondil
entities.short_description: Siriondil was the eleventh King of Gondor.
entities.description:
Siriondil was the eleventh King of Gondor.

Siriondil became King of Gondor in TA 748 after the death of his father Atanatar I. He had two sons, Tarannon and Tarciryan. His reign was without notable events and probably peaceful. He ruled for eighty-two years and died in TA 830 at the age of two-hundred and sixty years of age and was succeeded by his son, Tarannon.

The name Siriondil probably meant 'River- lover' or 'River-friend' in Quenya.

entities.name: Silmariën
entities.short_description: Silmariën was a princess of Númenór known as the ancestor of the Lords of Andúnië, and receiver of many heirlooms passed to her descendants.
entities.description:
Silmariën was a princess of Númenór known as the ancestor of the Lords of Andúnië, and receiver of many heirlooms passed to her descendants.

Silmariën was the oldest child of King Tar-Elendil. Her other siblings were Isilmë and Irimon. Women were not allowed to rule at the time of her father, so when Tar-Elendil relinquished the Sceptre, she was passed over for the throne in favor of her younger brother, Tar-Meneldur. After her marriage with Elatan, they had a son named Valandil who became the first Lord of Andúnië.

From her and her husband's lineage came the Kings of Gondor and Arnor living in exile in Middle-earth. She was one of the most significant members of Númenor's royal family, as she presumably inherited both the sword Narsil and the Ring of Barahir from Tar-Elendil, her father. These heirlooms were then handed down to her descendants, the Lords of Andúnië and later the Kings of Gondor and Arnor. The royal jewel, the Elendilmir, included a fillet of mithril that had once belonged to Silmariën, survived the Fall of Númenor to become the royal circlet of Arnor, and survived into the Fourth Age

Silmariën was a Quenya name that meant "silver maiden", from the words silma ("silver, shining white") and rien ("maiden, daughter"). Though unlikely, Silmariën could have meant "maiden crowned with silver", as the Sindarin word ríen means "crowned lady, queen".

entities.name: Pengolodh
entities.short_description: Pengolodh (or Pengoloð) was a Loremaster of the Ñoldor who dwelt in Gondolin.
entities.description:
Pengolodh (or Pengoloð) was a Loremaster of the Ñoldor who dwelt in Gondolin.

Pengolodh was born in Nevrast to a Ñoldorin lord and a Sindarin lady. Early tales about the Fall of Gondolin mention him as one of the lords of the city, and ruler of the Twin Folk of the Pillar and the Tower of Snow. As one of the Lambeñgolmor, he was known as the Sage of the Ñoldor and counted as the greatest Loremaster since Fëanor and Rúmil. He was also the tallest of the Elves of Gondolin.

Pengolodh escaped the sack of the city with Tuor and Idril's company of survivors and followed them to the Mouths of Sirion. He is not further mentioned in writing, but since the Inias Beleriand are attributed to him, as well as the edited Ínias Dor-Rodyn (furthering the work of Rúmil), he must have stayed in Lindon for at least a while after the War of Wrath, so that the Dúnedain could copy his work.

It was during his stay at the Mouths of Sirion that Pengolodh did the majority of his work. Is attributed to him the composition of the Lhammas and other prominent linguistic texts from ancient Middle-earth, in which he collected much material concerning also the mátengwië, the gesture-code of the Elves. Basing on information obtained from the refugees of Doriath, he made copies and extracts of documents written in Cirth, possibly preserving them as an active writing system.

entities.name: Ostoher
entities.short_description: Ostoher was the son of King Anardil of Gondor, and became the seventh King of Gondor upon his father's death in TA 411.
entities.description:
Ostoher was the son of King Anardil of Gondor, and became the seventh King of Gondor upon his father's death in TA 411.

He moved his summer residence from the capital city of Osgiliath to the fortress of Minas Anor in TA 420. During this time he rebuilt and greatly added to it and over time it would become a city as well as a fortress, until after the Great Plague of 1636 when it became the capital of Gondor, over twelve-hundred years later.

In the last two years of his reign the Easterlings started attacks on Gondor. Due to his advanced age, he sent his son Tarostar (later Rómendacil) to meet the Easterling threat, who was victorious.

Ostoher died in TA 492 at the age of two-hundred seventy after a rule of eighty-one years and was succeeded by Tarostar.

entities.name: Rómendacil I
entities.short_description: Rómendacil I was the eighth King of Gondor.
entities.description:
Rómendacil I was the eighth King of Gondor.

Rómendacil, initially named Tarostar, was the son of King Ostoher. When the Easterlings invaded in TA 490, Tarostar as crown-prince was charged with leading the defense against them, as Ostoher was too old. He succeeded his father upon his death in TA 492. Tarostar defeated the Easterlings, after many battles, by TA 500. After the victory he renamed himself Rómendacil, meaning "East-victor".

It was he that created the office of the Steward of Gondor, as a high councilor to the king. When the line of kings failed two thousand years later, the holders of this office would rule Gondor.

The peace on Gondor's frontiers was not to last forever: forty years later in TA 541 the Easterlings invaded once more, and Rómendacil rode to meet them in battle, but was slain.

entities.name: Orophin
entities.short_description: Orophin was a Silvan march-warden from Lothlórien, and the brother of Haldir and Rúmil.
entities.description:
Orophin was a Silvan march-warden from Lothlórien, and the brother of Haldir and Rúmil.

Orophin guarded the western border of Lothlórien at the time of the War of the Ring. He stood guard with other Elves, including his brothers Haldir and Rumil.

Like Rúmil, Orophin knew very little Westron; therefore, he associated little with the Fellowship of the Ring. When Haldir saw Gollum rustling through the trees near where the hobbits stayed for the night, Orophin left his brothers to warn the Galadhrim.

The name Orophin is either Sindarin or Silvan Elvish. It may mean "small tree", from Sindarin oron ("tree") and pîn ("small"), or "mountain peak", from orod ("mountain") and pind ("peak, crest").

entities.name: Rôg
entities.short_description: Rôg is part of lord of the rings.
entities.description:
Rog was an Elf-lord from the hidden city-realm of Gondolin during the First Age.

Rog was the Lord of the House of the Hammer of Wrath and the chief blacksmith in Gondolin. He was the strongest of the Gondolindrim, and the third greatest in valour. He died during the Fall of Gondolin, after putting up a valiant fight.

entities.name: Ondoher
entities.short_description: Ondoher was the thirty-first King of Gondor.
entities.description:
Ondoher was the thirty-first King of Gondor.

Ondoher succeeded his father Calimehtar in TA 1936. During his time the rulers of Gondor and Arthedain became aware that a power was coordinating attacks on the Exiles of Númenor, leading to the two kingdoms to renew contact and form an alliance. Ondoher's daughter Fíriel married Prince Arvedui of Arthedain. In TA 1944, the Wainriders invaded Gondor from the east while their allies, the Haradrim, invaded Gondor from the south. Ondoher and his eldest son and heir, Artamir, led the main army close to the Black Gate, where they clashed with the Wainriders. The left wing of Ondoher's army was commanded by Adrahil, the Prince of Dol Amroth. The right wing was commanded by Minohtar, the captain of Gondor's armies. The center was commanded by Ondoher himself.

In the ensuing battle Ondoher was slain together with Artamir, and Gondor was defeated. The rearguard of the army defended Ithilien while Adrahil joined up with General Eärnil, who had defeated the Haradrim.

Although Eärnil finally defeated the Wainriders, it was learned that Ondoher's second son Faramir (not to be confused with Faramir, brother of Boromir) was slain with his father, despite a law requiring that at least one heir should be left behind.

entities.name: Soronto
entities.short_description: Soronto was a Númenorean nobleman of the royal lineage of Númenor or House of Elros, the grandson of Tar-Meneldur and son of Ailinel, sister of Tar-Aldarion. He lived in the later years of the first millennium of the…
entities.description:
Soronto was a Númenorean nobleman of the royal lineage of Númenor or House of Elros, the grandson of Tar-Meneldur and son of Ailinel, sister of Tar-Aldarion. He lived in the later years of the first millennium of the Second Age. His father was Orchaldor, a descendant of the House of Hador.

Before the change in Númenor's law that turned the order of succession into cognatic primogeniture, Soronto may have been presumptive heir to the throne. (J.R.R. Tolkien intended to write a story about Tar-Aldarion's daughter Tar-Ancalimë and her cousin Soronto, and how she married only to prevent Soronto from inheriting the throne.)

The name Soronto apparently means "Eagle", "Eagle-friend", or perhaps "Man of the Eagle" in Quenya, from soron ("eagle").

{|class="mw-collapsible mw-collapsed" data-expandtext="Show" data-collapsetext="Hide" style="border: 1px solid #a6a6a6; width:65%;"

entities.name: Tar-Aldarion
entities.short_description: Tar-Aldarion was the sixth King of Númenor, and succeeded his father, Tar-Meneldur. Tar-Aldarion was married to Erendis, a Númenórean woman, who was not a direct descendant of the house of Elros as Aldarion himself, and…
entities.description:
Tar-Aldarion was the sixth King of Númenor, and succeeded his father, Tar-Meneldur. Tar-Aldarion was married to Erendis, a Númenórean woman, who was not a direct descendant of the house of Elros as Aldarion himself, and therefore had a shorter life-span. Aldarion's love for the sea ultimately caused a rift between the couple and they separated in SA 882. The tale of their marriage and estrangement survived the Downfall of Númenor as "Aldarion and Erendis: The Mariner's Wife".

Tar-Aldarion was called "The Mariner", and his name signifies "of the trees" because he was a noted tree steward and forester — trees were essential to the construction of his fleets, but he took great care to replenish what was being felled. His first love was the sea, and he was already a great explorer before he became king, founding the Guild of Venturers to promote exploration. He made several journeys to Middle-earth and established contact with Gil-galad in his realm in the Grey Havens making friendship and alliance with him. He also established the first Númenorean port in Middle-earth, named Vinyalonde, built on the river Gwathló, and during his reign the deforesting of Enedwaith and Minhiriath began.

His only child was a daughter, Tar-Ancalimë, so he changed the rules of succession, replacing the principle of agnatic primogeniture with that of fully equal primogeniture. She became the first ruling Queen of Númenor. If not for the change, the throne would have passed to his sister's son Soronto, heir presumptive at the time.

The partial story of Aldarion and Erendis can be found in Tolkien's , (ed. Christopher Tolkien). Though the actual story was left incomplete, the book does give some hints on how it continued. The story also contains the first hints of the return of the Shadow, i.e. Sauron, to Middle-earth.

entities.name: Nienna
entities.short_description: Nienna (Quenya; IPA or - "Weeping" or "She Who Weeps") was an Ainu, one of the Aratar and a Vala who was responsible for the mercy and grief spread across Arda. She was the sister of Mandos and Irmo and had no spouse.…
entities.description:
Nienna (Quenya; IPA or - "Weeping" or "She Who Weeps") was an Ainu, one of the Aratar and a Vala who was responsible for the mercy and grief spread across Arda. She was the sister of Mandos and Irmo and had no spouse. Her part in the Music of the Ainur was one of deep sadness, from which grief entered the world at its beginning. She had dominion over the Halls of Nienna, which were on the western edge of Valinor, looking over the sea.

Nienna was concerned with mourning, and she pitied the suffering of others, especially the Marring of Arda by Melkor. Yet the lesson of Nienna is not of endless grief, but rather of pity, hope, and the endurance of the spirit.

Nienna dwelt in far western Valinor near Mandos, and she seldom came to Váli-màr. Her windows looked out beyond the Walls of the Night.

During the creation of the Two Trees, she watered the mound with her tears.

entities.name: Maedhros
entities.short_description: Maedhros, also called Maedhros the Tall, was a prince of the Ñoldor, eldest of the seven Sons of Fëanor, and head of the House of Fëanor following the death of his father in Middle-earth. He was highly renowned for his…
entities.description:
Maedhros, also called Maedhros the Tall, was a prince of the Ñoldor, eldest of the seven Sons of Fëanor, and head of the House of Fëanor following the death of his father in Middle-earth. He was highly renowned for his skills as warrior and diplomat. For centuries, he led his House against the forces of Morgoth, but the Oath that he and his six brothers had sworn to recover the Silmarils constrained him and ultimately brought his demise.

Maedhros was born in Eldamar, probably in Tirion, to Fëanor and Nerdanel sometime during the Noontide of Valinor. It was noted that, of all Fëanor's sons, he alone bore semblance to his mother by way of his red hair. It would be seen throughout his life that he inherited too some significant portion of her temperament, as unlike most of his brothers, he generally was neither quick to anger nor rash in his actions.

After the flight of Fëanor from Tirion in Valinor, he went with his father to Formenos. When Morgoth killed Finwë and stole Fëanor's beloved Silmarils, Maedhros was the first son to take the terrible Oath of Fëanor to recover the holy jewels.

Maedhros participated in the First Kinslaying alongside his father and brothers. He was, however, the only one of Fëanor's sons to not participate in the burning of the Teleri ships, and he advocated for ships and oarsmen to return to Aman to ferry Fingolfin's host. When his father instead destroyed the ships, Maedhros did not object aloud, but instead stonily watched as the vessels burned. After landing in Middle-earth, the Ñoldor were attacked by an army of Orcs, leading to the Dagor-nuin-Giliath. The Elves were victorious and the remnants of the Orcish army retreated to Angband, pursued by Fëanor and a small vanguard. But Fëanor's force encountered a number of Balrogs as they approached Angband, and were quickly slain. Fëanor himself was dealt a mortal wound by Gothmog, the Lord of the Balrogs, but Maedhros and his brothers arrived with a relief force to rescue him. However, Fëanor died from his wounds soon thereafter.

entities.name: Míriel
entities.short_description: Míriel Therindë (also written Þerindë; later Serindë) was the first wife of Finwë, High King of the Ñoldor, and mother of Fëanor. Míriel's hair was described as being silver in appearance, an unusual color for one of…
entities.description:
Míriel Therindë (also written Þerindë; later Serindë) was the first wife of Finwë, High King of the Ñoldor, and mother of Fëanor. Míriel's hair was described as being silver in appearance, an unusual color for one of the Ñoldor.

Míriel married Finwë sometime during the Noontide of Valinor and they lived in Tirion. In YT 1169, Míriel bore a son, called Curufinwë, whom she called Fëanáro ("Spirit of Fire"). After giving birth to him she could no longer live, and so wished to die, something which was impossible because, as an Elf, she was immortal within Arda.

After Finwë was killed, Míriel was granted permission to return to life, and she entered the service of Vairë. Her task to weave all the deeds of the House of Finwë in the Tapestry of Time.

Míriel was described to have silver hair and a slender figure. Her customary singing while working was described as "soft and sweet".

entities.name: Mandos
entities.short_description: Mandos was an Ainu, one of the Aratar, and the Vala responsible for the judgement of the Spirits (or Fëa) of all Elven dead. He also had responsibility for pronouncing the dooms and judgments of Eru Ilúvatar under…
entities.description:
Mandos was an Ainu, one of the Aratar, and the Vala responsible for the judgement of the Spirits (or Fëa) of all Elven dead. He also had responsibility for pronouncing the dooms and judgments of Eru Ilúvatar under Manwë. His real name was Námo, but was called by the Elves Mandos after his sacred Halls of Mandos, over which he presided, to which Elves would go if they perished.

Mandos was the sixth greatest of the Lords of the Valar, and fifth greatest of the Aratar.

Mandos was the brother of Irmo (Lórien) and Nienna in the mind of Eru Ilúvatar. He and Lórien were the "Fëanturi", the Masters of Spirits. His wife was Vairë the Weaver.

It was he who pronounced Manwë's Doom concerning the espousals of the Eldar in YT 1172, when Finwë asked counsel for a second marriage after the death of his wife and her passing to the Halls of Mandos.

entities.name: Maglor
entities.short_description: Maglor was the second son of Fëanor and Nerdanel. He was the greatest poet and minstrel of the Ñoldor and was said to have inherited his mother's gentler temperament.
entities.description:
Maglor was the second son of Fëanor and Nerdanel. He was the greatest poet and minstrel of the Ñoldor and was said to have inherited his mother's gentler temperament.

Among the seven brothers, only Maglor, Caranthir, and Curufin were married, but nothing is told of their wives.

Maglor was born in Eldamar during the Noontide of Valinor in the First Age.

As with the other Sons of Fëanor, Maglor was bound by an oath to recover his father's Silmarils, stolen by the Dark Lord Morgoth. This oath took the seven brothers to Middle-earth during the late First Age where they established realms in exile, waged war against the armies of Morgoth, fought their own Elven kind, and eventually brought ruin upon themselves.

entities.name: Manwë
entities.short_description: Manwë (Quenya: "Blessed One") was the leader of the Ainur, one of the Aratar, King of the Valar, husband of Varda, brother of the Dark Lord Melkor, and King of Arda. He was also known as Súlimo, Mânawenûz, or Valahiru,…
entities.description:
Manwë (Quenya: "Blessed One") was the leader of the Ainur, one of the Aratar, King of the Valar, husband of Varda, brother of the Dark Lord Melkor, and King of Arda. He was also known as Súlimo, Mânawenûz, or Valahiru, and lived atop Mount Taniquetil in Valinor, the highest mountain of the world. The winds and airs were his servants.

He was the greatest in power of all the Valar, as Melkor, although more powerful than Manwë, had rebelled against the will of Eru Ilúvatar and as such, had set himself against his peers. It is said that Manwë was the only Vala who took counsel from Eru from time to time.

Manwë was eldest of the Ainur that best understood the will of Eru. Manwë by contrast was entirely unconcerned with his own power, and wished only to prepare the world for the coming of the Children of Ilúvatar. He oversaw all of the Valar's early attempts to order Arda, but was unable to stop Melkor's rampages until the Vala Tulkas came to Arda to assist his brethren.

Afterwards, the Valar under Manwë made an abode on Middle-earth in the Isle of Almaren and constructed the two Lamps of the Valar to provide light to the world. But Melkor destroyed the lamps, and the Valar retreated to the continent of Aman, which they heavily fortified. Eventually, the Elves awoke in Middle-earth, and Manwë at last went with the other Valar to subdue Melkor. They succeeded, and Melkor was imprisoned in the Halls of Mandos. He extended an invitation to the Elves to journey to Aman and live there amongst the Valar. For the three Ages of Melkor's imprisonment, the Valar and the Elves lived in peace and happiness. But eventually Melkor was allowed to plead for pardon before Manwë again.

entities.name: Nimrodel
entities.short_description: Nimrodel was a Nandorin Elf-maiden of Lórien in the Third Age.
entities.description:
Nimrodel was a Nandorin Elf-maiden of Lórien in the Third Age.

Nimrodel had lived in Lothlórien before the Sindar and Ñoldor were seen in the forest. She was unhappy with these newcomers, thinking they would bring the turmoils of Middle-earth to the golden forest. She lived separately near the river that would later bear her name, and spoke only her native tongue. The only good thing she saw in Lórien was the Sinda Amroth, King of the Wood. They both found love for each other, but she refused to marry him.

After a Balrog awoke in nearby Khazad-dûm in TA 1980, Nimrodel grew more uneasy in Lórien. She fled, and made her way to the edge of Fangorn Forest, but could not enter it. Amroth found her, and promised her peace. Together they travelled to Edhellond, the port city in Belfalas, and thence set sail to the Undying Lands. They were accompanied by a small staff of Silvan Elves, including Mithrellas. All went well until they reached the White Mountains in TA 1981. The group became separated, and Amroth reached Edhellond well before the others. He decided to wait for his love aboard their ship. When a storm broke loose and swept the ship out of port, Amroth leaped overboard, hoping to swim back to shore. But he was quickly taken by Belegaer's strong currents and drowned.

Nimrodel, in the meantime, had settled for a while at the river Gilrain, which reminded her of home. She sat by the starlit stream and slept for a long while. After waking she journeyed further, but found no ship in Edhellond, and Amroth was long dead at the bottom of the sea.

entities.name: Maeglin
entities.short_description: Maeglin was an Elf, the son of Eöl the "Dark Elf" and Aredhel, daughter of Fingolfin. He lived during the First Age of the Sun in Middle-earth, and was a lord of the hidden Elven kingdom of Gondolin. He became infamous…
entities.description:
Maeglin was an Elf, the son of Eöl the "Dark Elf" and Aredhel, daughter of Fingolfin. He lived during the First Age of the Sun in Middle-earth, and was a lord of the hidden Elven kingdom of Gondolin. He became infamous for his betrayal of the location of Gondolin to the Dark Lord Morgoth.

Aredhel had left Gondolin to wander through Beleriand, and in the woods of Nan Elmoth, she met Eöl, and stayed with him, eventually giving birth to Maeglin. Eöl gave his child the name Maeglin when he was twelve. His mother told him about Gondolin and its people throughout his childhood and he desired to see his related kin in the Hidden City. He and his mother soon grew weary and discontented with their life in Nan Elmoth and Eöl's strict shunning of the outside world. When Aredhel finally decided to leave Eöl, she took her son (who stole his father's sword, Anguirel, forged of meteor iron) with her and returned to Gondolin. However, Eöl had followed her, and in judgement before Turgon, he attempted to kill Maeglin with a poisoned dart, but hit Aredhel instead. She died, and Eöl was cast down to his death from the city walls.

Maeglin was now an orphan, but Turgon held him in honor, and Maeglin both learned and taught much. He became an elven-prince held in high esteem, even leading his own noble house. He found rich loads of metals in the Echoriad surrounding the city and forged weapons of steel stronger than had been seen before. His mine in the Echoriad was named Anghabar, "Iron Mine". In the Nírnaeth Arnoediad, Maeglin refused to remain behind as regent, and went forth to battle with Turgon. The seventh and final gate of Gondolin, the Great Gate of Steel, was Maeglin's creation.

Even though Maeglin was one of the mighty of Gondolin, his greatest desire was to take Turgon's daughter Idril to be his wife. But his desire was in vain, for Idril was his own first cousin, and as such was considered by Elven society to be too close in kinship with Maeglin to allow for any romantic relationship. Additionally, Idril was well aware of Maeglin's thoughts concerning her and despised him for it.

entities.name: Mahtan
entities.short_description: Mahtan was a renowned Ñoldorin metallurgist of Aman and the father of Nerdanel, the wife of Fëanor.
entities.description:
Mahtan was a renowned Ñoldorin metallurgist of Aman and the father of Nerdanel, the wife of Fëanor.

Mahtan was a skilled smith in Valinor who learned the arts of metal and stonework under direction of the Vala Aulë. He wore a copper circlet around his head and was known for his fondness for metal above gold. Mahtan passed on his knowledge to his eager pupil and son-in-law, Fëanor, who surpassed his teacher by becoming the greatest of all Elven craftsmen. When Fëanor and certain Ñoldor became more proud and suspicious of other Ñoldor kin due to the lies of Melkor, and began forging armaments for what would be Valinor's first war, Mahtan came to regret teaching him. Later, Nerdanel became estranged from Fëanor and retired back to Mahtan's house. The servants of Aulë counselled against joining the Revolt of the Ñoldor, and therefore Mahtan chose not to rebel, and remained in Valinor in peace forever after.

Mahtan had a beard, which was unusual for an Elf, especially a young one. J.R.R. Tolkien tells that Elves could only grow beards from the "third cycle" of their lives, while Mahtan was an exception, being only early in his second cycle. It is unclear what these "cycles" actually refer to.

The name Mahtan might be from the Quenya mahta- ("to handle"), referring to the arts and skill of making. His devotion to Aulë had earned him the name Aulëndur ("Servant of Aulë") from -ndur ("to serve"). The earlier form of this name was Aulëndil, which was later used by Sauron during his treachery to Númenor.
entities.image_credit: Fair-use identification thumbnail via Fandom. Character / franchise art © Tolkien Estate / New Line / Warner Bros. / Amazon (as applicable). Not free or redistributable artwork.

entities.name: Nerdanel
entities.short_description: Nerdanel (Quenya), also known as Nerdanel the Wise, was the daughter of the Ñoldorin smith Mahtan and the wife of the infamous Fëanor, eldest son of King Finwë.
entities.description:
Nerdanel (Quenya), also known as Nerdanel the Wise, was the daughter of the Ñoldorin smith Mahtan and the wife of the infamous Fëanor, eldest son of King Finwë.

Unlike her husband, she was of a peaceful nature and sought to moderate his fiery temper and pride with wisdom. For a time, she was the only one able to influence him.

Nerdanel refused to follow her husband to Middle-earth, and their parting was not a happy one. When it became clear that he intended to leave Valinor for good, she came to him and pleaded with him to let her youngest sons, Amrod and Amras, remain with her. Fëanor would hear nothing of it and accused her of being against him and in league with the Valar, namely Aulë. He stated that the sons wished to follow and obey their father; if she did not follow him she would be abandoning all of their children. She then scorned him saying that he would not have them all and then she left, possibly retiring to her father's house in Aman. By refusing to join her husband in revolt, Nerdanel avoided the Doom of Mandos, though her sons did not. The last remnant of her family to die was her grandson Celebrimbor, the forger of the three Elven Rings of Power in the second age.

Nerdanel was a sculptor of great note and is said to have made deceptively lifelike statues.

entities.name: Mardil Voronwë
entities.short_description: Mardil Voronwë was a noble Man of Gondor from the House of Húrin during the mid-Third Age, who held these offices:
entities.description:
Mardil Voronwë was a noble Man of Gondor from the House of Húrin during the mid-Third Age, who held these offices:

Mardil Voronwë was the son of the Vorondil, a great hunter of beasts. By his time the position of Steward of Gondor was already hereditary and Mardil received the title of Steward on the death of his father in TA 2029. His Stewardship began during the last part of the reign of King Eärnil II and throughout the reign of Eärnur, Eärnil's son.

During Eärnur's reign as king, Mardil was charged with the difficult task of restraining the desire of Eärnur to fight the Witch-king of Angmar, the chief of the Ringwraiths, who accused Eärnur after the Battle of Fornost of being afraid to fight him.

The King of Minas Morgul (one of the titles of the Witch-king of Angmar) reminded Eärnur of this and challenged him at the start of his reign in TA 2043. Although an angry Eärnur wanted to fight the Morgul lord he was restrained with difficulty by Mardil. However, when the Witch-king issued another challenge with great insult seven years later in TA 2050, Mardil could not restrain Eärnur, who then rode to Minas Morgul and was never seen again.

entities.name: Narmacil II
entities.short_description: Narmacil II was the twenty-ninth King of Gondor and the son of Telumehtar.
entities.description:
Narmacil II was the twenty-ninth King of Gondor and the son of Telumehtar.

In the second year of his reign a confederation of Easterlings called the Wainriders began to raid the eastern territories of Gondor. Five years later they invaded in force, overrunning the eastern territories. Narmacil marched to Rhovanion to fight the invaders but was utterly defeated and slain in the Battle of the Plains. He was one-hundred and seventy-two years old and ruled for only six years. He was succeeded by his son Calimehtar.

The name Narmacil is Quenya for 'fire-sword', from the words nár, meaning 'fire', and macil, meaning 'sword'.

entities.name: Malvegil
entities.short_description: Malvegil was the sixth King of Arthedain.
entities.description:
Malvegil was the sixth King of Arthedain.

Malvegil was the son of King Celebrindor of Arthedain and came to the throne in TA 1272 at the death of his father. Under his rule the enemy realm of Angmar was established by the Witch-king north of the Ettenmoors in the Mountains of Angmar, and evil things began to appear in Eriador. Many Orcs and evil Men began to gather on both sides of the Misty Mountains, and Arthedain was in an uneasy watch ever after. Malvegil died in TA 1349 at the age of two-hundred and five after ruling for seventy-seven years and was succeeded by his son Argeleb I.

The name Malvegil means "Golden sword" from the Sindarin words mal ("gold") and megil or later vegil ("sword").

entities.name: Minardil
entities.short_description: Minardil was the twenty-fifth King of Gondor.
entities.description:
Minardil was the twenty-fifth King of Gondor.

Minardil was born in TA 1454 during the reign of his great-grandfather Eldacar and was the son and successor of King Hyarmendacil II whom he succeeded in TA 1621. His reign was brief and turbulent. His steward, Húrin of Emyn Arnen, would found the line of the House of Húrin, who became Ruling Stewards centuries later. In TA 1634, he was at Pelargir when it was suddenly attacked by the Corsairs of Umbar and he was slain. Minardil ruled for thirteen years. He had two sons: his eldest son Telemnar (who succeeded him) and his younger son Minastan.

Minardil is a Quenya word that means 'Tower-lover', from Minas (mutated into Minar), and the suffix -(n)dil, meaning 'lover/devoted to'.

entities.name: Lothíriel
entities.short_description: Lothíriel was a princess of Dol Amroth in Middle-earth, daughter of Prince Imrahil, and later Queen of Rohan.
entities.description:
Lothíriel was a princess of Dol Amroth in Middle-earth, daughter of Prince Imrahil, and later Queen of Rohan.

Lothíriel was the wife of King Éomer of Rohan. Lothíriel was the daughter of Prince Imrahil of Dol Amroth; her mother's name is not known. Lothíriel was born in TA 2999. She had three older brothers: Elphir, Erchirion, and Amrothos. She was Boromir and Faramir's cousin.

Lothíriel married Éomer, King of Rohan, in TA 3021 They had at least one son named Elfwine the Fair, who became the nineteenth King of Rohan on the death of his father in the year 63 of the Fourth Age.

Lothíriel means "flower-garlanded maiden," from the Sindarin words loth ("flower, blossom"), and the element riel ("garlanded maiden"). The latter of the words comes from the root rig ("twine, wreathe"), and the feminine ending -iel.

entities.name: Narmacil I
entities.short_description: Narmacil I was the seventeenth King of Gondor after the death of his father Atanatar II Alcarin in TA 1226. Like Tarannon Falastur before him, he was notable for his childlessness.
entities.description:
Narmacil I was the seventeenth King of Gondor after the death of his father Atanatar II Alcarin in TA 1226. Like Tarannon Falastur before him, he was notable for his childlessness.

Narmacil was born in the year TA 1049 to Atanatar II and his unnamed wife. He was as lazy as his father and was soon tired of being king. Intending to pursue his own personal pleasures and activities, he created the office of Regent and surrendered practical rule to his nephew Minalcar by TA 1240 (who would eventually become king in his own right).

During his reign, the Easterlings started to become a threat again and his regent's main concern was making alliance with the tribes of the Northmen to help fight against them. Narmacil died childless in TA 1294 after reigning sixty four years and ruling for fourteen, he was succeeded by his brother Calmacil.

entities.name: Manthor
entities.short_description: Manthor was a Man of Brethil during the First Age. He was descended from Halmir, who was the fourth Halbar and the great-grandfather of Manthor through his mother Meleth.
entities.description:
Manthor was a Man of Brethil during the First Age. He was descended from Halmir, who was the fourth Halbar and the great-grandfather of Manthor through his mother Meleth.

Manthor was the son of Agathor and Meleth. He ran for Chieftain of the Men of Brethil against Hardang, because Manthor was related to Brandir the Lame, the previous Halbar of the Haladin, and Manthor thought that he could win by his noble blood, as Brandir was his second-cousin. However, Manthor was related to Brandir through Halmir's daughter Hiril, who was the grandmother of Manthor and the sister of Halmir's son Haldir, who in turn was the grandfather of Brandir. This meant that Manthor's kinship with Brandir was worth less in the eyes of the people of Haleth, and he lost the election. And Hardang too was related to Brandir, as Brandir was his second-cousin through Halmir's other son Hundar, the brother of Haldir and the grandfather of Hardang. Hence, Hardang was the victor in the election, and he appointed Manthor to be the Master of the North-march at the Crossings of Taeglin. Sagroth, Daruin, and Forhend were some who were under his authority.

At Haudh-en-Elleth, he and his company once came across weary Húrin, and brought him to the Hall of the Haladin, fulfilling Húrin's errand. At the Hall, the Halbar Hardang tried to attack Manthor as they were of opposing houses. Húrin managed to wound Hardang, and after an imprisonment was forced to stand trial for it, at the 301st Folkmoot of Judgment. Manthor successfully defended Húrin there, and revealed Hardang's corrupted loyalty to the people, which led to a revolt.

Manthor died in woods next to Nen Girith, by an arrow-wound from Daruin, who earlier had turned against him and broken his command. This took place after the revolt at the trial, during which Daruin had tried three times to slay Manthor with an arrow.

entities.name: Nolondil
entities.short_description: Nolondil was the third son and youngest child of Vardamir Nólimon, second King of Númenor.
entities.description:
Nolondil was the third son and youngest child of Vardamir Nólimon, second King of Númenor.

Nolondil's eldest brother became the third King of Númenor, Tar-Amandil. His father Vardamir was potentially Half-elven like his grandfather Elros, the first King of Númenor. This means he may have been a Half-elf of the third generation, giving him a slow maturity and long youth like the Elves, while being fated for mortality like Men. Nolondil married and had three children children: one daughter, Yávien, and two sons, Oromendil and Axantur.

Nolondil means "Devoted to knowledge" in Quenya from ñólë ("lore, knowledge") and -ndil ("friend, lover, devoted to").

entities.name: Meleth
entities.short_description: Meleth was a woman of Brethil during the First Age.
entities.description:
Meleth was a woman of Brethil during the First Age.

Meleth was the child of Hiril and Enthor. She was the wife of Agathor, to whom she bore Manthor and Hunthor.

entities.name: Meneldil
entities.short_description: Meneldil was the third King of Gondor (his father Anárion and uncle Isildur co-ruled Gondor as the second kings, but his father died before Isildur who was sole ruler for a short time).
entities.description:
Meneldil was the third King of Gondor (his father Anárion and uncle Isildur co-ruled Gondor as the second kings, but his father died before Isildur who was sole ruler for a short time).

Meneldil was born in Númenor a year before its fall. The only son and fourth child of Anárion, he was said to be the last child born in Númenor before its downfall. He had three older siblings, all sisters.

After the War of the Last Alliance in which his father Anárion was slain, Meneldil was groomed by his uncle Isildur for a few years to rule Gondor, since Isildur and his sons intended to go north to rule Arnor. According to , Meneldil was farsighted and well-pleased at the planned departure of Isildur and his sons, hoping that affairs in the north would keep them occupied. Meneldil became the third King of Gondor in TA 2, about 4 years after the death of Anárion, after the death of Isildur in the Disaster of the Gladden Fields. Meneldil was the first King of Gondor who ruled independently from the High Kingdom of the Dúnedain, Arnor.

It is uncertain whether Meneldil was King by right, as young cousin Valandil would have had the better claim as High King of Gondor and Arnor, but no claim by Valandil was ever made. It was in any case unlikely that Meneldil would give up his right to rule to a much younger cousin he had never seen. In any case, the people of Gondor did not resist Meneldil's claim to the throne, and King Valandil and his heirs made no serious attempt to regain control over Gondor until the death of King Ondoher and his heirs. In effect, Meneldil thus severed Gondor from Arnor, but the title of High King remained with the northern line.
entities.image_credit: Fair-use identification thumbnail via Fandom. Character / franchise art © Tolkien Estate / New Line / Warner Bros. / Amazon (as applicable). Not free or redistributable artwork.

entities.name: Manwendil
entities.short_description: Manwendil was the third child and second son of Elros Tar-Minyatur, the first King of Númenor.
entities.description:
Manwendil was the third child and second son of Elros Tar-Minyatur, the first King of Númenor.

Manwendil was born after SA 61 and was the elder brother of Atanalcar and the younger brother of Tindómiel and the short reigning king Vardamir Nólimon. Nothing else is known of his life except for that he was possibly married and had children.

In The Nature of Middle-earth J.R.R. Tolkien considered making the children of Elros Half-elves, giving them the same choice of mortality as the Half-elven children of Elrond. Whether he adopted this idea fully is unclear.

Manwendil means "Devoted to Manwë" from the Quenya suffix -ndil ("friend, devoted to").

entities.name: Gothmog
entities.short_description: Balrogs ( ) are a species of powerful demonic monsters in J. R. R. Tolkien's Middle-earth. One first appeared in print in his high-fantasy novel The Lord of the Rings, where the Company of the Ring encounter a Balrog…
entities.description:
Gothmog was the primary Lord of Balrogs during the First Age, and the greatest Balrog ever to walk Middle-earth. He was High-captain of Angband, being Morgoth's front-line lieutenant as well as one of his most important servants. He fought many battles in the name of his master, and was personally responsible for killing two of the High Kings of the Ñoldor.

Gothmog, like the rest of his kind, carried a fiery whip into battle, but was also known for wielding a great black axe, feared by Elves across Beleriand.

Gothmog was initially one of the Maiar who gave their allegiance to Melkor. Prior to the revolt of the Ñoldor, he was High Captain of Angband, given the title "Lord of Balrogs."

During the Dagor-nuin-Giliath in YT 1498, Fëanor pressed on to Angband with just a small company, and in that hour, the Balrogs issued forth. Gothmog was among them. Fëanor came even within sight of Angband, but was ambushed with few Elves about him. Soon he stood alone, but long he fought on alone against all the Balrogs. But at the last Gothmog, Lord of Balrogs, smote him to the ground, inflicting a mortal wound, and the High King of the Ñoldor fell. The Sons of Fëanor arrived and carried the body of their father away, but Fëanor had passed. Gothmog reappeared as a general of Angband in several more major conflicts, including the Dagor Aglareb and the Nírnaeth Arnoediad. During the Nírnaeth, Gothmog engaged the High King of the Ñoldor, Fingon, in battle. Gothmog separated Fingon from the main host but was unable to kill Fingon (in earlier versions) until the second and lesser Balrog lord Lungorthin appeared behind the Ñoldorin king and "cast a throng of steel about him". This allowed Gothmog to slay Fingon and beat the body to dust. Thereafter, he captured Húrin, father of Túrin Turambar and dragged him back to Angband.
entities.image_credit: Fair-use identification thumbnail via Fandom. Character / franchise art © Tolkien Estate / New Line / Warner Bros. / Amazon (as applicable). Not free or redistributable artwork.

entities.name: Idril
entities.short_description: Idril, also called Celebrindal, was a Ñoldorin Elf of Gondolin. She was the daughter of Turgon and Elenwë, wife of the Man Tuor, and mother of Eärendil the Mariner, a Half-elven.
entities.description:
Idril, also called Celebrindal, was a Ñoldorin Elf of Gondolin. She was the daughter of Turgon and Elenwë, wife of the Man Tuor, and mother of Eärendil the Mariner, a Half-elven.

Idril Celebrindal was the only child of Turgon, whose wife Elenwë perished during the crossing of the Helcaraxë. Together with Angrod's son Orodreth and Curufin's son Celebrimbor, she was one of three Ñoldor in the third generation to come into exile. Idril was loved in secret by her cousin Maeglin, the son of Eöl the Dark Elf and Aredhel, Turgon's sister, but she scorned his advances because of his dark character, as well as the fact that they were too closely related.

When Tuor, son of Huor, arrived in Gondolin, Idril fell in love with him. Because Turgon had grown to love Tuor as a son (as he had his father before), he allowed Idril and Tuor to wed, thus bringing about the second union of Men and Elves, after Beren and Lúthien. Their son Eärendil was born shortly afterwards.

Being far-sighted she sensed danger and she encouraged Tuor to prepare a secret way under the city so that if the city was attacked survivors could safely escape. After the Fall of Gondolin, Idril and Tuor became leaders of the exiles at the Mouths of Sirion in West Beleriand in the region of Arvernien, where they also received Elwing, daughter of Dior.
entities.image_credit: Fair-use identification thumbnail via Fandom. Character / franchise art © Tolkien Estate / New Line / Warner Bros. / Amazon (as applicable). Not free or redistributable artwork.

entities.name: Hador
entities.short_description: Hador Goldenhead, known also as Hador Lórindol, was a great chieftain of the Edain in the First Age of Middle-earth, and a revered Edain among many of the greatest Elf-friends of the Eldar. He became the first Lord of…
entities.description:
Hador Goldenhead, known also as Hador Lórindol, was a great chieftain of the Edain in the First Age of Middle-earth, and a revered Edain among many of the greatest Elf-friends of the Eldar. He became the first Lord of Dor-lómin and was accounted mighty even among the Eldar. Hador and his wife Gildis had three children: Glóredhel the first child and only daughter, Galdor, and Gundor.

Hador was the son of Hathol and the great-great-grandson of Marach (who first led the people of the Third House into Beleriand and was their first chieftain), and heir to the House of Marach. He entered the service of Fingolfin, the High King of the Ñoldor, at a young age. Hador was loved by the King, and he rose high in the esteem of many of the Eldar. Eventually, Hador would even become a part of Fingolfin's own council. Realizing the need for the Edain to live under their own lords and have lands of their own, Fingolfin granted as a fief to Hador the land of Dor-lómin (land of echoes) which thus made him the first Lord of Dor-lómin. Hador gathered most of the people of the Third House into that land, which lay in Hithlum. There, Hador's people became numerous, and he encouraged the use of the Sindarin tongue.

Hador continued to win renown among the Eldar as the Lord of Dor-lómin, as well as among Men. Two of Hador's children, Galdor and Glóredhel, were wedded to two of the children of Halmir, Chieftain of the Haladin, respectively Hareth, his daughter, and Haldir, his son of the House of Haleth, when the two peoples met for a great feast. Fingolfin also gave to Hador a great helm made by Telchar of Nogrod. It was made in the likeness of the dragon Glaurung and came to be known as the Dragon-helm of Dor-lómin; it could only be borne by one of great stature and strength. In the year 455 of the First Age, Morgoth broke the Siege of Angband in the Dagor Bragollach. Hador fought alongside Fingolfin with what few warriors of the Third House he could gather against the swift onset of Morgoth's forces. He was slain, however, defending the retreat of his lord. His younger son, Gundor, fell beside him before the fortress of Barad Eithel. It was said that their deaths were greatly mourned by the Eldar.

Hador was the forefather of many heroes. His grandsons were Húrin and Huor. His great-grandsons were Túrin and Tuor, and his great-great grandson was Eärendil the Mariner. Aragorn Elessar, as well as all the Kings of Númenor, Gondor and Arnor were descended from Hador. Perhaps the greatest testament to the legacy of Hador was that which was later written about his descendants:

entities.name: Ilmarë
entities.short_description: Ilmarë (Quenya) was chief amongst the Maiar and the handmaiden to Queen Varda.
entities.description:
Ilmarë (Quenya) was chief amongst the Maiar and the handmaiden to Queen Varda.

She was the handmaiden of Varda (thereby a guardian spirit of the stars) and one of the chiefs of the Maiar, along with Eönwë, the herald and banner-bearer of King Manwë.

In Quenya, Ilmarë means "Starlight", from ilma. Christopher Tolkien has noted that Ilmarë is related to such words as Ilmen and Ilmarin. It also resembles Ilmarinen, a character from Kalevala, one of Tolkien's influences.

Earlier in the growth of J.R.R. Tolkien's legendarium, Manwë and Varda, both called with the title of Wanwavoisi, were the parents of Ilmarë and Eönwë, that in this version were named Erinti and Fionwë Úrion. Tolkien later abandoned this idea of the Children of the Valar.

entities.name: Imrahil
entities.short_description: Imrahil, also known as Prince Imrahil, was the twenty-second Prince of Dol Amroth. He had two older sisters, Ivriniel and Finduilas. His daughter Lothíriel wedded Éomer, King of Rohan, in the last year of the Third Age.
entities.description:
Imrahil, also known as Prince Imrahil, was the twenty-second Prince of Dol Amroth. He had two older sisters, Ivriniel and Finduilas. His daughter Lothíriel wedded Éomer, King of Rohan, in the last year of the Third Age.

Born in TA 2955, Imrahil was the only son of Adrahil, twenty-first Prince of Dol Amroth. He succeeded the fief at the death of his father in TA 3010. Married to an unknown wife, he had three sons, Elphir, Erchirion and Amrothos and a daughter, Lothíriel. Legolas said of him that:

On March 9, TA 3019, Prince Imrahil led a company of Swan Knights and 700 men at arms to Minas Tirith to help defend the city. Prince Imrahil led the sortie that rode to the aid of Faramir and the rear-guard who were retreating from Osgiliath when the forces of Sauron overran the Pelennor Fields on March 13. Gandalf rode with them, and the Winged Nazgûl fled before Gandalf's light. The Knights of Dol Amroth rescued Faramir from the Southrons but he was poisoned, and Imrahil carried his nephew back to Minas Tirith on his horse. Gandalf then took command of the besieged city, and Prince Imrahil assisted him because Denethor in his madness retreated to the White Tower with his son in the belief he was dying, paying no further attention to the city's defense.

During the Siege of Gondor, Imrahil and Gandalf made circuits of the Othram, bolstering the defenders before taking command of the defense of the Great Gate. On March 15th, with the arrival of Rohan, the defenders proceeded to sortie from the city to link up with them, with Imrahil leading the attack in the Battle of the Pelennor Fields.

entities.name: Indis
entities.short_description: Indis a Vanyarin Elf-maiden of Valinor and second wife of Finwë, King of the Ñoldor.
entities.description:
Indis a Vanyarin Elf-maiden of Valinor and second wife of Finwë, King of the Ñoldor.

She was the niece of Ingwë, King of the Vanyar and High King of the Elves, for her mother was his sister. Indis was known for her great beauty and was thus referred to as Indis the Fair.

In YT 1185, Indis married Finwë, High King of the Ñoldor, and was his second wife after the death of Míriel Serindë. She bore two sons, Fingolfin and Finarfin, and two daughters, Findis and Irimë. Through Finwë's first marriage, she was the stepmother to Fëanor, his first and only son to Míriel.

Unfortunately, Fëanor harbored very little love for her or her sons which probably contributed to his mistrust of Fingolfin when Melkor began spreading his poisonous lies amongst the Ñoldor.

entities.name: Ingwë
entities.short_description: Ingwë was the Vanyarin Elf who held titles of King of the Vanyar and High King of the Elves. He dwelt in Ingwemar with the rest of his House. He was the uncle of Finwë's second wife Indis.
entities.description:
Ingwë was the Vanyarin Elf who held titles of King of the Vanyar and High King of the Elves. He dwelt in Ingwemar with the rest of his House. He was the uncle of Finwë's second wife Indis.

Ingwë was born in Cuiviénen during the Years of the Trees to Ilion, a direct descendant of Imin and Iminyë. After Oromë discovered the Quendi, Ingwë was part of the first embassy to Aman alongside his friends Finwë and Elwë, and became the lord of the first Kindred of the Elves, the later Vanyar, who led his people in the Great Journey. His name means "first one / chief" in Quenya.

First of the Vanyar to travel to Valinor with Oromë, Ingwë loved its beauty and bliss and, returning to his people, urged them to undertake a journey to Aman. He and his kin took the journey, were fascinated with the Valar, and decided not to return to Middle-earth. They stayed and made Ingwë their king. The Mindon Eldaliéva, in Tirion, was built in honor of him.

Ingwë was reckoned as High King of all the Eldalië, the Elves of the Great Journey, and was therefore called Ingwë Ingweron, the "Chief of the Chieftains". He lived on Taniquetil, ruling under Manwë, High King of Arda.

entities.name: Huan
entities.short_description: Tolkien, J.R.R., (Kindle Location 582). Houghton Mifflin Harcourt. Kindle Edition.
entities.description:
Tolkien, J.R.R., (Kindle Location 582). Houghton Mifflin Harcourt. Kindle Edition.

Huan, the Hound of Valinor, was a great Wolfhound of the First Age. He was given by the Vala Oromë the Hunter to his friend Celegorm, one of the Sons of Fëanor. Huan was as large as a small horse, and accompanied Celegorm on his huntings. When the Ñoldor under Fëanor rebelled, Huan went with his master to Middle-earth.

Huan had been granted special powers by the Valar, and was allowed to speak three times before he died. It was also prophesied that he could not be killed unless it was by the greatest wolf that ever lived.

Huan was originally a Hound of Oromë in Valinor and was eventually given to Celegorm, Fëanor's third son. He went into exile with his master during the Flight of the Ñoldor. He might have stayed with his master in Himlad and later fled with him to Nargothrond after their defeat in the Dagor Bragollach.

entities.name: Hallas
entities.short_description: Hallas was the thirteenth Ruling Steward of Gondor.
entities.description:
Hallas was the thirteenth Ruling Steward of Gondor.

Hallas was born in TA 2480 and was the son of Cirion. When Cirion died in TA 2567, Hallas succeeded him as Ruling Steward. Calenardhon had been given by his father to the Éothéod, and Hallas grew particularly friendly with the new arrivals and devised the names Rochand and Rochirrim for the land and its people, which became Rohan and Rohirrim in the Sindarin dialect of Gondor. In effect, Gondor had been halved in size, but it had gained a strong ally to the north in return.

War never ceased on Gondor's eastern borders as the Balchoth were not completely destroyed, but they were no longer a serious threat. More of a problem was the Corsairs of Umbar, who kept raiding the coasts and Orcs based in Minas Morgul.

Hallas died in TA 2605 at the age of 125 years old after thirty-eight years of rule. He was succeeded by his son Húrin II.

entities.name: Húrin I
entities.short_description: Húrin I was the fifth Ruling Steward of Gondor.
entities.description:
Húrin I was the fifth Ruling Steward of Gondor.

Húrin was born in TA 2124, and was the son of Belegorn. He was descended from Húrin of Emyn Arnen, one of the stewards in the days of the Kings of Gondor and founder of the House of Húrin. His name was taken in the likeness of Húrin, hero of the Edain in the Elder Days and father of Túrin Turambar.

Following the death of his father in TA 2204, Húrin I became the fifth Ruling Steward of Gondor, and the fifth steward to rule during the era known as the Watchful Peace. Húrin I held the stewardship for forty years until his death in the year TA 2244 at the age of 120 years old. Húrin I was succeeded by his son Túrin I.

The name Húrin means "Steadfast" in Sindarin.

entities.name: Húrin II
entities.short_description: Húrin II was the fourteenth Ruling Steward of Gondor.
entities.description:
Húrin II was the fourteenth Ruling Steward of Gondor.

Born in TA 2515, Húrin II was the son of Hallas. Húrin II succeeded his father as Steward in TA 2605. Sporadic warfare on Gondor's eastern and southern borders continued. Other than minor skirmishes no events are recorded during his rule. Húrin II died in TA 2628 after twenty-three years of rule at the age of 113 years old. He was followed by his son Belecthor I.

Húrin was named after a host of ancestors and great heroes: Húrin I, his ancestor, Húrin of Emyn Arnen, the founder of the House of Húrin, and Húrin Thalion, hero of the First Age and father of Túrin Turambar.

The name Húrin means "Steadfast" in Sindarin.

entities.name: Landroval
entities.short_description: Landroval was one of the Great Eagles of Middle-earth and the brother of Gwaihir the Windlord.
entities.description:
Landroval was one of the Great Eagles of Middle-earth and the brother of Gwaihir the Windlord.

Landroval was a descendant of Thorondor. It was said that Landroval and his brother Gwaihir helped Thorondor rescue Beren and Lúthien from Angband.

During the Third Age, Landroval was part of the rescue mission to save Thorin and Company from burning trees and it was possible that he fought in the Battle of Five Armies with the other Great Eagles.

Landroval assisted Gwaihir in his many associations with Gandalf and his companions. He was present at the Battle of the Black Gate, swooping to attack the Nazgûl on their Fellbeasts. Together with Gandalf, Gwaihir and Meneldor, he also rescued Frodo Baggins and Samwise Gamgee from Mordor after the completion of the Quest of the Ring.
