entities.short_description: Forhend was a Man of Brethil, and a guard of the Crossings of Taeglin, in the First Age.

entities.name: Galdor of the Tree
entities.description:
Galdor was an Elf of Gondolin in the First Age.

Galdor was the Lord of the House of the Tree. He was a great warrior, second only to Turgon in valor. He followed the House of Turgon during the Exile of the Ñoldor. He fought in Kinslaying at Alqualondë. When he arrived in Middle-earth, he fought in the Battle of the Lammoth and Dagor Aglareb. When Turgon built the city of Gondolin, he followed Turgon and settled in Gondolin. He became the lord of the House of the Tree. He then joined Gondolin's army and fought in the Nírnaeth Arnoediad. The house of the Tree was large, and it (along with the house of the Hammer of Wrath) was the first to confront the enemy in the Fall of Gondolin. Galdor fought with an iron-studded club and may also have used a sling like others in the House of the Tree. Galdor and his house fought a long war against the forces of Morgoth. And in the wrath of their onset, they caused the Orcs to "fall like leaves."

Galdor saved the lives of Tuor and Ecthelion during the Fall of Gondolin. Tuor, bearing the wounded Ecthelion, came to the Square of the Folkwell, which Galdor and his Elves were defending. As Tuor came he stumbled beneath Ecthelion and fell; had it not been for Galdor coming to his aid, Tuor and Ecthelion would have been slain by the Orcs. He was leading the company of refugees but was attacked by an ambushing Orc-party. Despite the surprise of the attack, he fought off the Orcs efficiently, though he lost some of his kin, who were mostly killed by falling rocks rather than Orcs.

Galdor escaped the Fall of Gondolin and came to the Mouths of Sirion with the other refugees. He survived the onslaught of the Sons of Fëanor in the Third Kinslaying. After he fought in War of Wrath he migrated to the island of Tol Eressëa and reportedly still lives there.
entities.short_description: Galdor was an Elf of Gondolin in the First Age.

entities.name: Gereth
entities.description:
Gereth was one of the Elves who aided the flight of Evranin from Artanor (the place which would later become Doriath) during the years following the battles between Elves and the Nauglath. They bore the Necklace of the Dwarves away from the sons of Fëanor.

Gereth and Evranin are not mentioned in the final story of the Necklace of the Dwarves in The Silmarillion.

Category:Elves of Doriath Category:Grey Elves Category:Precanonical Elves Category:Elves Category:Characters in The History of Middle-earth Category:Elves of Beleriand

entities.name: Gilfanon
entities.description:
Gilfanon a·Davrobel was a Ñoldorin Elf of Tol Eressëa.

Gilfanon was one of the oldest living Elves on Tol Eressëa. He lived in the House of the Hundred Chimneys in the town of Tavrobel. He knew the Elf Lindo and was present when Lindo hosted the Man Eriol at the Cottage of Lost Play during his time on the island. During one night, Gilfanon told Eriol the tale of the Sun and the Moon as they spoke together.

He was also known for recounting a tale of the exile of Ñoldor and the coming of Men.

Gilfanon is a Gnomish name with an unknown meaning, though the first word may be derived from the Sindarin word Gil ("star").
entities.short_description: Gilfanon a·Davrobel was a Ñoldorin Elf of Tol Eressëa.

entities.name: Gorgol
entities.description:
Gorgol, also called the Butcher, was an Orc captain in Sauron's service who lived in Beleriand during the First Age.

Gorgol's service to Morgoth's chief agent, Sauron, had earned him the moniker of "the Butcher". After Gorlim's betrayal, Gorgol was sent as captain of Sauron's warband to slaughter Barahir and his companions near Tarn Aeluin. After "butchering" the outlaws, he claimed the famous Ring of Barahir as "Old Sauron bade [him] bring it back."

Believing his master had "no lack of weightier treasures in his hoard", the greedy Gorgol, holding the hand of Barahir aloft, said that he was minded to keep the Ring and declare to Sauron that the hand of Barahir was bare. But at that moment Beren, son of Barahir, sprang into the camp, slew Gorgol, and seized the hand, making his escape.

entities.short_description: Gorgol, also called the Butcher, was an Orc captain in Sauron's service who lived in Beleriand during the First Age.

entities.name: Gostir
entities.description:
Gostir was the name of one of the dragons of Morgoth, about whom very little is told.

Gostir is a Ñoldorin name meaning "dread-glance", containing the elements gost ("dread, terror") and thîr ("look, face, expression, countenance"), as well as the root thē, meaning "look (see or seem)".

Gostir appears as a white Cold-drake with red eyes who dwells north of Rhûn in Barl Syrnac in the Creatures of Middle-earth supplement of Middle-earth Role Playing. Gostir was said to be the older brother of Lhamthanc.

entities.name: Hendor
entities.description:
Hendor was a house-carle and servant of Idril Celebrindal during the First Age. It is told that Hendor carried Eärendil, when he was a child, to safety amid the Fall of Gondolin when they, Tuor, and others were assailed by wolf-riders.

entities.name: Ingwion
entities.description:
Ingwion was a Vanyarin Elf, the son of Ilwen and Ingwë, High King of the Elves.

Ingwion was born in Cuiviénen to Ingwë and Ilwen during the Years of the Trees. He had one younger sibling and was a cousin of Indis. After the Great Journey, when he and his kindred came to Aman, they first dwelt in Tirion, but soon came to love the full light of the Two Trees, and relocated to Valinor at the base of Taniquetil. Ingwion likely dwelt there for many years with his family.

In the year 545 of the late First Age, Ingwion was the leader of the Vanyar who came with the Host of the Valar to Middle-earth to fight in the climatic War of Wrath.

During the war, Ingwion was the leader of a force of Vanyar Elves tasked with retaking Eglarest. They were successful in driving the Orcs away from the shores during the battle.
entities.short_description: Ingwion was a Vanyarin Elf, the son of Ilwen and Ingwë, High King of the Elves.

entities.name: Ivárë
entities.description:
Ivárë was once a renowned minstrel of the Elves.

Because he was called "who plays beside the sea" or "piper of the sea", he was likely one of the Solosimpi, the Elves that lived in the shores of Aman. He was counted among the greatest minstrels of the Elves, along with Maglor, Daeron, and Tinfang, and one of the most 'magic' dancers, along with Tinfang and Tinúviel.

Ivárë is a Qenya name with an untold meaning. Ior was its cognate in Gnomish.

Category:Falmari Category:Quenya names & words Category:Characters in The History of Middle-earth Category:Precanonical Elves
entities.short_description: Ivárë was once a renowned minstrel of the Elves.

entities.name: Langon
entities.description:
Langon, also known as the Shadow Messenger, was a servant of Melkor appearing in the earliest version of the legendarium given in The Book of Lost Tales.

Langon was originally a servant of Námo, but became a renegade before being perverted by Melkor.

When the Valar besieged Utumna in the Great Lands after Melkor had locked himself inside by shutting the huge gates in their faces, Tulkas tried and failed to break them down before Oromë blew them open instantly with his horn. After hearing Manwë's immeasurable voice bidding him to to issue forth at the gates, Melkor became doubtful and remained in hiding "deep down within Utumna". Instead, the Dark Lord sent his servant Langon to the gates to negotiate with the Valar, claiming that only the herald of Manwë, Nornorë, can enter and speak to Melkor. However, Langon caused the wrath of the Valar because his message was full of insolence and flattery.

After Melkor destroyed the Two Trees, Langon was sent to "the gates of Valmar" in Valinor as a messenger to state Melkor's demands and to confuse the Valar. When he demanded to speak to all of the Valar, they asked who sent him there. When Langon revealed his servitude to Melkor, Tulkas wanted to kill him by hurling "stones from the walls", byut was overruled by the other Valar despite their shared anger. They allowed Langon leave to speak in "the great square of gold that was before Aulë's courts". When all of the Valar and the Elves were settled there, Langon did not speak immediately, but rather moved next to "the needle of pure gold" that contained Aulë's "story of the kindling of the Tree of gold". It was only after being commanded by Manwë that Langon spoke his message.
entities.short_description: Langon, also known as the Shadow Messenger, was a servant of Melkor appearing in the earliest version of the legendarium given in The Book of Lost Tales.

entities.name: Lhamthanc
entities.description:
Lhamthanc, was the name of a serpent, about whom almost nothing is known. It is possible that the word serpent may actually be referring to one of the dragons of Morgoth since Tolkien often described dragons as worms and serpents.

Lhamthanc was a serpent only known to possess a serpent-name, and possibly may be one of the dragons of Morgoth.

Lhamthanc is a Ñoldorin name meaning "forked tongue", being derived from the elements lham(b) ("tongue") and thanc ("cleft, split"), as well as the root lab ("lick").

Lhamthanc was originally called Iamthanc, an early Ñoldorin name meaning "snake, (lit) forked tongue", being derived from the elements lham(b) ("tongue") and thanc (" cleft, divided, split, cloven, forked, bifurcated; cleft, break, breach"). However, Tolkien eventually settled on Lhamthanc for the name.
entities.short_description: Lhamthanc, was the name of a serpent, about whom almost nothing is known. It is possible that the word serpent may actually be referring to one of the dragons of Morgoth since Tolkien often described dragons as worms…

entities.name: Lindo
entities.description:
Lindo was a Ñoldor Elf of Tol Eressëa, and the owner and keeper of the Cottage of Lost Play in early stages of J.R.R. Tolkien's mythology.

Lindo lived in the cottage with his wife Vairë where they both entertained many visitors, including the Man Ælfwine (Eriol) who visited there.

He was known to be very wise in many things, and once told to Eriol the tale of the Sun and Moon's creation.

entities.name: Littleheart
entities.description:
Littleheart, also known as Ilverin and the Gong-warden, was an Elf of Tol Eressëa in the earliest version of J.R.R. Tolkien's legendarium.

Much of Littleheart's early life is untold, save only that he was the son of Bronweg, and obtained his name due to "the youth and wonder of his heart". He was known to be ancient beyond count, being either fifty or ten thousand years of age.

Sometime near the end of the First Age, Littleheart gained possession of the gong, Tombo. During the Third Kinslaying in YS 534, Littleheart was among one of the only survivors.

Later, he accompanied Eärendil's final voyage on Vingilot in seeking for Kôrtirion. While traversing the Shadowy Seas, Littleheart rang his gong to wake up the Sleeper in the Tower of Pearl on Tol Withernon, the westernmost of the Twilit Isles.
entities.short_description: Littleheart, also known as Ilverin and the Gong-warden, was an Elf of Tol Eressëa in the earliest version of J.R.R. Tolkien's legendarium.

entities.name: Brytta Léofa
entities.description:
Brytta, also known as Léofa, was the eleventh King of Rohan.

Born in TA 2752, Brytta was the son of Fréaláf Hildeson. He became king at the age of forty-six when his father died in TA 2798.

During his reign, Rohan was still recovering from its war with the Dunlendings, and hostilities remained at the western borders. Brytta possessed a generous nature and was always willing to help those in need, because of his generous and kind spirit he earned the epithet Léofa, which means Beloved, in the Rohanese tongue. Aside from the troubles with the Dunlendings his rule saw a new trouble, as the War of the Dwarves and Orcs caused great numbers of Orcs to flee from the Misty Mountains, the Orcs sought to make strongholds and refuges in the White Mountains south of Rohan.

The Orcs made war on the people of Rohan, and Brytta fought off their incursions into Rohan and the White Mountains. The campaigns of Brytta against the Orcs were so successful that when he died it was believed that Rohan was free of Orcs.
entities.short_description: Brytta, also known as Léofa, was the eleventh King of Rohan.
entities.image_credit: Fair-use identification thumbnail via Fandom. Character / franchise art © Tolkien Estate / New Line / Warner Bros. / Amazon (as applicable). Not free or redistributable artwork.

entities.name: Maidros
entities.description:
Maidros, or Golfinweg, was a Ñoldorin Elf who was the father of Bruithwir (the precursor to Finwë) and the grandfather of Fëanor according to the early version of the legendarium in .

J.R.R. Tolkien's accounts of this character went through several revisions. In fact, "Golfinweg" was reused as the name of Finwë, who was made the father of Fëanor; while the name Maidros was partially reused for the character of Maedhros, the first son of Fëanor. Furthermore, the father of Finwë remained unnamed. It is possible that Fëanor named his son after his grandfather.

Category:Characters in The History of Middle-earth Category:Gnomish names & words Category:Ñoldor Category:Precanonical Elves

entities.name: Meril
entities.description:
Meril was a Sindar Elf of the North (Northerland) who became the wife of Orodreth and mother of Finduilas and Gil-galad.

After the expulsion of Curufin and Celegorm, Meril was sent away by Orodreth with their young son Gil-galad to the Falathrim in Eglarest, due to the fear "that all strong places were doomed to fall at last before the might of Morgoth".

Meril is the Sindarin word for "rose", used as a name.

Category:Characters in The History of Middle-earth Category:Elves of Nargothrond Category:Sindar Category:Sindarin names & words
entities.short_description: Meril was a Sindar Elf of the North (Northerland) who became the wife of Orodreth and mother of Finduilas and Gil-galad.

entities.name: Morwë
entities.description:
Morwë, along with Nurwë, refused the summons of the Valar to Aman.

Upon discovering the awakening of the Elves in Cuiviénen, the Vala Oromë traveled back to Valinor to bring news. When Oromë returned to the Elves, he invited them. Ingwë, Finwë, and Elwë served as their ambassadors. The ambassadors returned three years later to persuade the other Elves to come to Aman. Morwë and Nurwë refused the summons, leading the Avari in Cuiviénen.

The Quenya mor means ("black") and the suffix -wë occurs in many names, though not exclusively masculine.

Category:Avari Category:Characters in The History of Middle-earth Category:Elves
entities.short_description: Morwë, along with Nurwë, refused the summons of the Valar to Aman.

entities.name: Naimi
entities.description:
Naimi or Nelmir, also known as Earissë, was an Elf of Tol Eressëa.

After Ælfwine drank the limpë, he returned young and became immortal and married Naimi. The couple had two sons: Heorrenda and Hendwine.

The meaning of Naimi/Nelmir in Early Quenya is unclear.

According to the versions of the legendarium, Naimi was alternatively the daughter or the niece of Vairë and Lindo.
entities.short_description: Naimi or Nelmir, also known as Earissë, was an Elf of Tol Eressëa.

entities.name: Nielíqui
entities.description:
Nielíqui was a Vala, the daughter of Oromë and Vána in earlier forms of the legendarium.

Little is known about Nielíqui save that she was a small maiden who often danced in her father's woods. The Vala Òmar was known to sing in gardens of Oromë nearby while she danced.

Category:Valar Category:Characters in The History of Middle-earth Category:Precanonical Ainur
entities.short_description: Nielíqui was a Vala, the daughter of Oromë and Vána in earlier forms of the legendarium.

entities.name: Nimloth of Doriath
entities.description:
Nimloth was an Elf of Doriath during the First Age. She was the daughter of Galathil, son of Galadhon, the son of Elmo. Elmo was the brother of Olwë and Elwë, making her a kinswoman of King Thingol.

Nimloth married Dior the Fair, her second cousin. In the few years before the death of Thingol, she lived near the waterfall of Lanthir Lamath at the base of the Blue Mountains. Her children Eluréd, Elurín and Elwing were born there.

When Thingol died, she traveled to Doriath with her husband and their children and became Queen of Doriath. She was later slain in the Kinslaying of Menegroth by the Sons of Fëanor along with her husband. Elwing escaped to the Havens of Sirion but it is unknown whether her brothers survived or not. It was tradition among the Laiquendi of Ossiriand that they were led to safety by the birds and beasts after being abandoned in the forest by the servants of Celegorm.

In Sindarin, the name Nimloth means "white flower", from the words nim ("white") and loth ("flower, blossom"). Her name might also mean "Pale blossom".
entities.short_description: Nimloth was an Elf of Doriath during the First Age. She was the daughter of Galathil, son of Galadhon, the son of Elmo. Elmo was the brother of Olwë and Elwë, making her a kinswoman of King Thingol.

entities.name: Nurwë
entities.description:
Nurwë was an Elf from Cuiviénen who refused the summons of the Valar.

When the three ambassadors of the Elves, Ingwë, Finwë, and Elwë, returned from Aman, they invited the other Elves to travel there. However, Nurwë and Morwë refused, thus leading the Avari left behind.

The Quenya term nur or nura means ("to separate") and -wë may have come from -wego which is frequent in masculine names.

Category:Avari Category:Characters in The History of Middle-earth Category:Elves
entities.short_description: Nurwë was an Elf from Cuiviénen who refused the summons of the Valar.

entities.name: Ómar
entities.description:
Ómar, also known as Amillo, was a Valar in the earlier forms of the legendarium. His character was discarded rather quickly; he barely made it past The Book of Lost Tales.

Ómar was youngest of the Valar and the brother of Salmar when he entered into the world lastly. He was a master of languages and knew all tongues and sang great songs for all to hear. He was known to be singing and trilling in the gardens of Oromë near the Woods of Oromë where Nielíqui (the daughter of Oromë and Vána) danced. He was later involved in the decision to capture Melko and participated in the war with his brother Salmar and the other Valar. When the Elves later came to the Aman, the Teleri learned much of song from him. When darkness fell upon Aman, he spoke of the "lamentation of Vána" referring to her sadness over the loss of Laurelin.

Category:Valar Category:Characters in The History of Middle-earth Category:Precanonical Ainur

entities.name: Orcobal
entities.description:
Orcobal was an Orc of Angband that was slain by Tuor in Gondolin during the First Age.

During the Fall of Gondolin, Orcobal was the champion of the Orcs that assailed the Gondothlim alongside the Balrogs at the coming of the Drakes. Orcobal was ultimately slain by Ecthelion of the Fountain, who, after killing two goblin captains, "cleft the head of Orcobal their chiefest champion to his teeth", before the gates of Gondolin. The slaying of Orcobal was part of the famous onslaught which is said to have been the greatest killing of Orcs ever conducted by the Eldar.

Orcobal is clearly Gnomish, though it is not glossed.

entities.name: Penlod
entities.description:
Idril, Earendil, Tuor, Salgant, Penlod, Duilin, and Rog, by Kazuki Mendou

Penlod was an Elf-lord of Gondolin in the First Age.

Penlod was the marshall of two Gondolin houses, the Tower of Snow and the Pillar, and was the tallest of the Gondolindrim. He is not mentioned in the Silmarillion chapter concerning Gondolin's fall; rather, he appears only in The Book of Lost Tales Part Two.

During the Fall of Gondolin, the Elves of the city suffered a hard attack from the enemy after the death of Rog and the House of the Hammer of Wrath. Having to retreat further back into the city, Penlod perished "in a lane with his back to the wall", and with him many of his men.

entities.name: Poldor
entities.description:
Poldor was a man of Númenor according to the early version of the legendarium in The Lost Road.

Poldor was a peer of Herendil who lived during the reign of Tar-Calion, possibly being one of the sons of the friends of Elendil, Herendil's father. Like many of the Númenóreans of that time, he had no love of the Elves and Elf-friends of the First Age. Herendil complained to his father that Poldor had called him Eärendel the previous day by way of scorn or mockery.

Poldor is a name in Quenya meaning "breaker up of the hard/tough" or "land-breaker", being derived from the root pol ("can, have physical power and ability; pound up, break up small, reduce to powder").

In earlier drafts of the Quenya language, the name Poldor was derived from pol in polda ("strong, burly").
entities.short_description: Poldor was a man of Númenor according to the early version of the legendarium in The Lost Road.

entities.name: Ragnor
entities.description:
Ragnor was an Edain man of Dorthonion and one of the XII Bëorings who followed Barahir in the First Age.

After the Dagor Bragollach, Ragnor remained with Barahir and his company who refused to surrender or submit to the will of Morgoth, thus they became outlaws surviving for nearly five years. He and the others were eventually betrayed to Sauron by the unhappy Gorlim and killed at Tarn Aeluin.

entities.name: Rían of Gondor
entities.description:
Rían was the daughter of the Steward Barahir. When her brother the Steward Dior died childless and thus without an heir, her son Denethor I became the new Ruling Steward of Gondor. Her fate is unknown.

Her name may have been influenced by the Edain woman Rían, the wife of the First Age hero Huor.

The name Rían means "Crowned gift" in Sindarin, from the words rî ("crown") and ann ("gift").

Category:Characters in The History of Middle-earth Category:Men of Gondor

entities.description:
Saelon the Wise was an Edain woman during the First Age.

Saelon was the daughter of Malach and Zimrahin.

entities.name: Sagroth
entities.description:
Sagroth was an Edain of Brethil during the First Age.

Sagroth was under the command of Hardang the Halbar.

He encountered Húrin at the Haudh-en-Elleth during the time of Húrin's wanderings.

entities.name: Salgant
entities.description:
Salgant was the Lord of the House of the Harp in Gondolin. He was heavy and squat and owned a harp of gold. He presided over a noble house of valiant warriors loyal to the realm and the King but had character flaws. Despite his inadequacies, he was a friendly Elf and knew Eärendil as a child; he often played with him and taught him to play music with the wooden pipes he made for him. He was said to have fawned on Maeglin and was a craven coward.

Unfortunately, Salgant was a traitor and was persuaded by Maeglin to join in his conspiracy to seize the kingship of Gondolin for himself, though the prospect frightened Salgant. In furtherance of this, he used his position to persuade Turgon to hold the city at all costs. When the attack came, the King ordered Salgant to defend the Great Market with Glorfindel and his house of Elves. In an act of betrayal, he countermanded that order and sent his warriors to the Lesser Market instead, but they rebelled.

He fled in fear and disappeared. His fate is unknown. Eärendil mourned for him when he heard that his childhood friend was not amongst the survivors.

entities.name: Sangahyando
entities.description:
Sangahyando was the great-grandson of Castamir of Gondor and along with Angamaitë, he became an important figure amongst the Haradrim and the Corsairs of Umbar.

Sangahyando, like Angamaitë, was probably born in Umbar to an unnamed mother and father. As descendants of the rebel Castamir, they carried on the traditional hatred against Gondor. In TA 1634, when King Minardil was at Pelargir, spies of Sangahyando and Angamaitë told them about the king's visit to the city. They launched a surprise attack, killing the king and sacking the city. His ultimate fate is unknown.

Sangahyando was a Quenya word that meant 'throng-cleaver'. Sangahyando was originally called "Sangahyanda" in an earlier text.

entities.name: Tarannon
entities.description:
Tarannon "Falastur" was the twelfth King of Gondor.

Tarannon succeeded his father Siriondil in TA 830. His brother was Tarciryan. He started the construction of Gondor's navies, and became known as the first of the Ship-kings. Under his policies and successful rule, Gondor's extended its power to the west and south of the Mouths of Anduin. He, along with Narmacil I, was one of two childless Kings of Gondor, making him a break-point in the bloodline. Nevertheless his rule was marked by such vigorous naval expansion that at his coronation he assumed the additional [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regnal_name regnal name] of Falastur, meaning 'Lord of the Coasts'.

The king particularly favored the city of Pelargir, constructing a palace there built out over the Anduin river on arches.

Despite his successes, his reign was troubled by the intrigues of his own wife Queen Berúthiel who spied on everyone within the kingdom. Eventually, he grew tired of her acts, exiling her and her cats to the south. As a result of his wife's exile, he died childless in TA 913, and was succeeded by his nephew Eärnil I.
entities.short_description: Tarannon "Falastur" was the twelfth King of Gondor.

entities.name: Tarondor of Gondor
entities.description:
Tarondor was the twenty-seventh King of Gondor.

Tarondor was the son of Minastan, and succeeded his uncle King Telemnar, who died in the Great Plague of TA 1636. Coming to the throne when he was still relatively young, he was the longest-reigning King of Gondor.

The Plague had devastated Gondor, and Tarondor strove to slowly rebuild it and its power. He pursued a policy of strict retrenchment, in which many outposts were abandoned. The most significant event in his reign was the removal of the capital from the now depopulated Osgiliath, to Minas Anor (later known as Minas Tirith) and the replanting of the White Tree. Gondor at this time was drained of its resources and manpower and could no longer afford to tend to the forts guarding the ancient entrances to Mordor. The fortresses were abandoned, paving the way for evil things to return. During his reign, the garrisons and outposts in Enedwaith were also abandoned, with Gondor's western frontier retreating to the Gap of Calenardhon and the White Mountains.

Tarondor died in TA 1798, after one-hundred and sixty-two years of rule. He was succeeded by his son Telumehtar later that year.
entities.short_description: Tarondor was the twenty-seventh King of Gondor.

entities.name: Thû
entities.description:
In an early stage of J.R.R. Tolkien's mythology, Thû was a temporary replacement of the villain Tevildo, Lord of Cats. He was known as the "Lord of werewolves" and "Necromancer", and was a precursor to the character Sauron.

As seen in Beren and Lúthien, Thû was treated as the first appearance of Sauron, while Tevildo is treated as a separate minion of Morgoth (though its history in the development of Sauron's character is mentioned in a footnote).

entities.name: Tulkastor
entities.description:
Tulkastor was a follower of the Vala Aulë. He dwelt long with the Teleri in the early days of the Elves on the island. He married an unnamed woman of unknown kindred and their child was Vairë, wife of Lindo, who was the caretaker of the Cottage of Lost Play.

In the development of tales, Tulkastor's name was originally Turenbor, and then Tulkassë.

entities.name: Tórin
entities.description:
Tórin, also known as Daurin, was a Ñoldorin Elf of Valinor in earlier versions of J.R.R. Tolkien's legendarium.

Tórin was a kinsman of Fëanor. When Melko and Gwerlum came to destroy the Two Trees of Valinor, Tórin attempted to stop them. However, the fallen Vala cut off one of Tórin's legs, and Gwerlum threw a web around him before Melko slew him. Then Melko used Tórin's blade, laced with the black, poisonous blood of Gwerlum, to destroy the silver tree Silpion.

Tórin is a Qenya name, and Daurin is its equivalent in Gnomish. Its meaning is unspecified.

Category:Precanonical Elves Category:Ñoldor Category:Characters in The History of Middle-earth Category:Quenya names & words

entities.name: Tû
entities.description:
Tû is a character of earlier versions of J.R.R. Tolkien's legendarium.

Tû appeared in a fragmentary version of Tolkien's working notes for the Coming of Men, given in The Book of Lost Tales Part Two as "Gilfanon's Tale". Tolkien apparently decided not to incorporate the tale into his mythos, as it did not survive to become part of the chapter of The Silmarillion entitled "Of the Coming of Men into the West".

Tû is described as a "wizard" or "fay" who ruled the Dark Elves of the further east of Middle-earth, around Cuivienen, just before the making of the Sun. One of his subjects, Nuin "Father of Speech", came to a hidden valley of great loveliness and found there sleeping figures young but not children, boys and girls: the Fathers of Men. He told this to Tu, who fell into great fear of the One, and told Nuin that these were the Fathers of Men, who were to be undisturbed. Notes then tell that Nuin awoke two of the Sleepers, Ermon and Elmir, and taught them speech; that Tû and Nuin shepherded the Sleepers when they awoke with the Sun, and that Men split into factions in the years afterward. Tû grew to shun day and took to dwelling underground. A demon named Fankil, son of Melkor, arose and set Men at each other's throats, and especially against the Elves. The folk of Ermon stood with the Elves, but Tû came forth and destroyed Fankil, and was buried under falling hills.

What race or manner of being Tû was is unknown; he was described a great magician and a being of power, benevolent but testy, and afterwards came to have great hatred of Men for the deeds they did to his Elves.
entities.short_description: Tû is a character of earlier versions of J.R.R. Tolkien's legendarium.

entities.name: Uin
entities.description:
Uin, known as the Great Whale and Gulma's great whale, was the primeval whale of Arda that served the Vala Ulmo.

During the Elder Days, when Ulmo gathered "a host of the greatest fish" to Tol Eressëa, Uin, "the mightiest and most ancient of whales", came among them alongside narwhals and sea lions. Ulmo directed them in using their strength to pull the island across Belegaer to the shores of Hísilómë in Beleriand. Once the Teleri were on the island, Uin and the rest of the host took them to the Bay of Faëry in Valinor before pulling the island back to Hísilómë.

On the trip back to Hísilómë, Ossë noticed Uin pulling the island and was jealous that his island was being used without his permission. Yet when he tried to pursue Uin, he was left far behind because Uin and the rest of the host were granted "the might of the Valar" by Ulmo. Thus, they reached Hísilómë again where the Noldoli got in the island. The second ferrying went as well as the first, save only for a minor annoyance from Ossë.

After the Noldoli were safely in Aman alongside the Teleri, Uin and the other great fish pulled the island for a final trip for the Solosimpi. However, "Ossë cast storms and shadows" to hinder a third trip, causing Ulmo to direct Uin through "devious ways", resulting in the great fish arrive late to Hísilómë. On the return trip back to Aman, Uin and the great fish were waylaid by Ossë and Uinen just as "the mists of the Shadowy Seas" were in sight. Ossë grabbed the island with his great hand, causing Uin, with all his great strength, to only be able to "scarcely drag it onward" since none of the Valar could beat Ossë with strength in water. With Uinen's aid, the island was anchored to the seafloor by making giant ropes out of the centuries old "leather-weeds and polyps" that grew "to unimagined girth" throughout the pillars of Ossë and Uinen's "deep-sea house".

entities.name: Urthel
entities.description:
Urthel was an Edain of the House of Bëor and one of the XII Bëorings who followed Barahir in the First Age.

After the Dagor Bragollach, Urthel remained with Barahir and his company, who refused to surrender or submit to the will of Morgoth, and thus they became outlaws, surviving for nearly five years in the barren highlands above the forest of Dorthonion, then in the hands of Morgoth. He and the others were eventually betrayed to Sauron by the unhappy Gorlim and killed at Tarn Aeluin.

entities.name: Valandil of Andúnië
entities.description:
Valandil founded the line of the Lords of Andúnië in the western region of Andustar on Númenor.

Valandil's father was Elatan of Andúnië, and his mother was Silmariën, eldest child of Tar-Elendil of Númenor. The laws of Númenor at that time would not allow Silmariën to rule as queen, so Valandil and subsequent Lords of Andúnië were not in line for royal succession.

By the end of the Second Age, however, Valandil's descendants would become kings in Middle-earth, beginning with Elendil, the last Lord of Andúnië and first High King of Arnor and Gondor.

Valandil was also the name of the youngest son of Isildur and the grandson of Elendil, who eventually became High King of Arnor.
entities.short_description: Valandil founded the line of the Lords of Andúnië in the western region of Andustar on Númenor.

entities.name: Valwë
entities.description:
Valwë, also called Gwalweg, was a Ñoldorin Elf of Tol Eressëa in early stages of J.R.R. Tolkien's mythology.

Valwë fled to the Great Lands along with the other Gnomes of Tol Eressëa in order to help Salmar free the Elves enslaved by Melko after the Fall of Gondolin. The Elves were utterly defeated in the Battle of Tasarinan, but Valwë managed to survive and return to Tol Eressëa alongside Tulkastor and Ingil, where he would eventually be the father of Lindo.

Valwë is a name in Qenya possibly meaning "the happy (or fortunate) one". Valwë translated to Gwalweg in Gnomish.

Christopher Tolkien mentioned in his commentary that though Valwë was originally written as Manwë, the name may have been a mistake.
entities.short_description: Valwë, also called Gwalweg, was a Ñoldorin Elf of Tol Eressëa in early stages of J.R.R. Tolkien's mythology.

entities.name: Zimrahin
entities.description:
Zimrahin was the wife of Malach, whom she wedded in the year FA 337. After their marriage, she took the elvish name Meldis. She bore Malach a daughter, Adanel, in FA 339, and a son, Magor, two years later.

Meldis was the Sindarin name for Zimrahin, which means friend.

In the 'Folk of Marach' family tree from The War of the Jewels, Zimrahin and Malach had a third child. Originally (in version one of the table) there was a note for multiple children that said, "Others not concerned in these Chronicles". In version two of the table this became one name, "Sael..th" that was changed to "Saelon", though this was subsequently struck out.

entities.name: Herefara
entities.description:
Herefara was a Rohirrim warrior who served King Théoden during the War of the Ring. He fought and died in the Battle of the Pelennor Fields.

His name was remembered in the song of the Mounds of Mundburg.

Herefara is Old English for "war-traveler".

In , Herefara comes from the town of Woodhurst in the Stonedeans, a province in western Rohan where many men have a mix of Rohirrim and Dunlending ancestry. His grandparents are Briant and Reeve Heremond; and his parents are Cynethryth and Herubrand. Under the influence of Saruman, in early March TA 3019 a conspiracy of men attacks the Reeve's family in the Mead Hall of Woodhurst. Heremond and Cynethryth are slain but Herubrand, who is wounded, is saved by his loyalist who hide him and his mother outside the city. They enlist the player, an outsider who could not have been involved the attack, to help them in uncovering the conspiracy and eventually take back the control of his city. Herefara is not present during these events, as he is leading the defense of Brockbridge, a village ruled by Háma's father Léoferth to the south from the forces of Isengard. Herubrand and Herefara later meet in the Drúadan Forest during the ride of the Rohirrim towards Minas Tirith. Herefara joins the player in patrolling the lands around beacons Nardol and Eilenach. During the Battle of the Pelennor Fields the father and son fight side by side but are slain by Gothmog's Orcs.

entities.name: Hugin
entities.description:
Hugin was a Man from Lake-town who attended the Council of Elrond.

He is not a character from J.R.R. Tolkien's books.

Hugin is featured as a card in . His name originates here.

In , the man pictured on Hugin's TCG card is present at the Council of Elrond, defends the position of Boromir regarding the critical question of who is to carry the One Ring to Mordor. He is a background character, and is not credited with the name.

entities.description:
Járnsmid was a merchant from the city of Dale.

During the War of the Ring, Járnsmid was sent as an emissary to attend the Council of Elrond, discussing what it is to be done with the One Ring.

entities.name: Linnar, Sindri, and Uri
entities.description:
Linnar, Sindri, and Uri were three non-canonical Dwarves of the Second Age, who each received one of the Dwarven Rings of Power.

They were created in the The Lord of the Rings Trading Card Game and were each royal lords after they received their Rings. The mined for Mithril, as well as Gold and Silver. Their Rings eventually faded, but it is not known whether they were eaten by dragons or fell into the hands of Sauron.

Sindri, Uri, and Linnar were portrayed by Rich Mayberry, Gino Acevedo, and Xander Forterie.

entities.name: Léowyn
entities.description:
Born in Aldburg, Léowyn wanted to become a Rohirrim warrior when she showed her skills with a light spear at an early age, but her father would not allow it. After the Battle of Helm's Deep, Léowyn attended the celebration at Meduseld where she and the attendants would honor the victims (both Men and Elves) that were killed while defending the Keep from Saruman's army of Uruk-hai. As Sauron was preparing to send his armies to attack Minas Tirith, the capital of Gondor, Léowyn, like Éowyn, disguised herself as a soldier and rode to the relief of Minas Tirith. She fought in the Battle of the Pelennor Fields and was mostly likely slain.

entities.name: Robin Smallburrow
entities.description:
Robin Smallburrow, nicknamed Cock Robin, was a long-standing Shirriff of the Shire at the time of the end of the Third Age and during Sharkey's occupation of the Shire.

Robin became Shirriff in TA 3012. Though having joined the Shirriffs earlier than Sharkey's occupation, when questioned by Samwise Gamgee on his role Robin replies that he only applied for the post of Shirriff as a means of wandering the Shire, talking with folks and "knowing where the good beer was." Like many Shirriffs during Sharkey's Scouring of the Shire, Robin Smallburrow is forced to continue service against his will as a part of the Shirriff's First Eastfarthing Troop in the town of Frogmorton. However, during the Hobbits uprising against their foreign oppressors, it is assumed that Smallburrow defects in order to help the hobbits.

After Sharkey's demise and the effort and work to return to norm within the Shire, very little is recorded of Smallburrow and his role or family within the Shire, though it is assumed that he, like the hobbits who lived at the start of the Fourth Age, enjoyed the years of plenty and prosperity that dawned over the Shire.

He was likely good friends with Samwise Gamgee, as Sam would name his twelfth child, Robin Gamgee, after him.

entities.name: Adrahil I
entities.description:
Adrahil I was a Prince of Gondor who lived around TA 1944 in the land of Belfalas.

Adrahil was born sometime before TA 1944 and was of traceable Númenórean lineage. He served King Ondoher of Gondor as a general during the Wars of the Wainriders in the year 1944.

Adrahil was descended from a Númenórean noble house that settled in Belfalas in the Second Age. Because of this, it is assumed he was an ancestor of Imrazôr, Galador and the Princes of Dol Amroth.

When King Ondoher led his army to face the Wainriders who threatened Gondor, Adrahil commanded the army's left wing. The soldiers of the right wing were under the command of the King's nephew Minohtar, while the centre was commanded by the king himself and his heir Artamir.
entities.short_description: Adrahil I was a Prince of Gondor who lived around TA 1944 in the land of Belfalas.

entities.name: Amloth
entities.description:
An Amloth, or Ambalotsë, was a crested helm, especially one worn by an Elf-lord such as Egalmoth in battle. The crest was typically of a flower or flowers.

Amloth is a Sindarin noun meaning "uprising flowers" from the elements am ("up, upwards, upon") and loth ("flower").

Ambalotsë is a Quenya noun meaning "uprising-flower" from the elements amba ("upwards") and lótë ("flower").

Category:Objects Category:Sindarin names & words

entities.description:
The Circles of the World, sometimes called the Confines of the World, has various meanings depending on the context of its usage, but generally means the confines of Arda and not the Timeless Void, more specifically Middle-earth (excluding Aman) after the Changing of the World, late in the Second Age. suggests that when capitalized (), it refers to all of Eä within the scope of the Ainulindalë ("The Music of the Ainur").

entities.name: Hallow of Eru
entities.description:
The Hallow of Eru was a sacred location in J.R.R. Tolkien’s legendarium, specifically mentioned in , particularly in the section titled Akallabêth, which recounts the downfall of Númenor.

The Hallow of Eru was a consecrated area on the summit of the Meneltarma, the central mountain of Númenor. It was dedicated to Eru Ilúvatar, the supreme deity of Tolkien's universe. This place is considered so holy that:

The Hallow of Eru represents the direct connection between Númenor and the divine will of Ilúvatar. It is a symbol of humility, reverence, and the proper relationship between mortals and the divine. Its sanctity contrasts sharply with the later corruption of Númenor, when the kings began to reject the Valar and Eru, leading to the island’s eventual destruction.

As the Númenóreans grew more prideful and sought immortality, they abandoned the worship of Eru and ceased to ascend the Meneltarma. This spiritual decline was a key factor in their downfall, as described in Akallabêth. The Hallow thus serves as a poignant reminder of the lost grace and the consequences of forsaking divine guidance. Category:Locations
entities.short_description: The Hallow of Eru was a sacred location in J.R.R. Tolkien’s legendarium, specifically mentioned in , particularly in the section titled Akallabêth, which recounts the downfall of Númenor.

entities.name: Angbor
entities.description:
The Angbor, also known as the Halabor or just the Stone, was the judgment seat in the Moot-ring of the Forest of Brethil, during the First Age.

The Angbor was a large, flat stone upon which the Halbar would sit upon during Folkmoots. It was located in the middle of the seat-filled Moot-ring, the place where Folkmoots were held by the Haladin. The accused would stand before the Angbor facing the Halbar and the assembly.

In the late First Age, Húrin Thalion stood accused facing the Angbor during the 301st Folkmoot for Judgement.

Angbor and Halabor were names in the Halethian language, both possessing the element bor ("Stone").
entities.short_description: The Angbor, also known as the Halabor or just the Stone, was the judgment seat in the Moot-ring of the Forest of Brethil, during the First Age.

entities.name: Market-place
entities.description: Lake-town, also known as Esgaroth, features a notable Market-place. This Market-place is characterized by a round pool connected to the lake by a waterway for boats. It is surrounded by wooden quays with steps and ladders leading down to the water. The greatest houses of Lake-town, including the Great House where the Master of Lake-town held feasts, are situated around this Market-place.

entities.name: Outlands
entities.description:
The Outlands, also known as Western Gondor, or the Southern Fiefs of Gondor, were the coastal lands south of the White Mountains, the regions of Gondor outside the Pelennor Fields.

These lands along the Bay of Belfalas provided several resources including fish from the Ethir Anduin, flowers from Lossarnach, and stone from the foothills of the mountains. There were also skilled soldiers who lived in these fiefs.

The Anfalas and Pinnath Gelin were collectively known as further Gondor.

After the Great Plague, the Corsairs of Umbar raided Gondor's coasts up to Anfalas, until Umbardacil retaliated, and retook Umbar in TA 1810.
entities.short_description: The Outlands, also known as Western Gondor, or the Southern Fiefs of Gondor, were the coastal lands south of the White Mountains, the regions of Gondor outside the Pelennor Fields.

entities.name: Crown of the Hidden Kingdom
entities.description:
The Crown of the Hidden Kingdom was the great king-helm of Turgon, the King of Gondolin.

A huge image of the Crown of the Hidden Kingdom was set in diamonds and placed above the midmost pillar of the Gate of Steel, the last of the Seven Gates of Gondolin. The gate would open inwards on either side of the pillar with the Crown of the Hidden Kingdom above it.
entities.short_description: The Crown of the Hidden Kingdom was the great king-helm of Turgon, the King of Gondolin.

entities.name: Timeless Void
entities.description:
The Timeless Void, also known as the Outer Void, was a conception of the state of Not-being, outside Creation or Eä. It should not, however, be confused with the conception of vast spaces within Eä, especially those conceived to lie all about the enisled Kingdom of Arda.

Eru Ilúvatar dwelt in the Timeless Halls, which were separate from the Timeless Void. Before the creation of Eä, Morgoth searched the Timeless Void thoroughly for Airefëa, the source of Eru's creative power, but was unsuccessful. It is believed that many creatures originated in the Timeless Void due to the discords in the Music of the Ainur caused by Morgoth.

After Eä was created, the Timeless Void still existed beyond it. At the same time, Eä contained vast spaces within itself, which separated Arda from many other, unknown worlds, where the other Ainur laboured, but their numbers and names were unfathomable for the minds of the Children of Ilúvatar. Only the Valar could know them.

Later, after his downfall in the War of Wrath, the Dark Lord Morgoth was cast out through the Door of Night into the Timeless Void, i.e. outside Time and Space and outside Eä altogether;

entities.name: Currency in Gondor
entities.description:
The Castar (S. Mirian) was the chief currency used within Gondor. A smaller coin was the tharni (S. canath), a silver coin worth a fourth of the castar.

Castar is a Westron word that resembles the word kast in Hobbit-speech and the word kastu in Rohanese, which both mean "mathom". Mirian is a Sindarin word that seems to be derived from mîr ("jewel").

In the 2014 video game , a Castar is the twenty-eighth collectable artifact: the Gondorian Coin. It is found high up on the side of the first ruined tower west of the Haedir in the Fern Outskirts region of the Sea of Núrnen. The Gondorian Coin was a specific Castar, a coin in Gondor, that dated to around the year 2920 of the Third Age. Castars like the Gondorian Coin were widely used by merchants throughout Middle-earth. The Doors of Durin and the great forge of Khazad-dûm featured on the coins in honor of the Dwarves who provided the mithril to make them. The coins became rare relics after Sauron destroyed most of them.

entities.name: Gaurin
entities.description: Gaurin appears in The Lay of the Children of Húrin (published in The Lays of Beleriand, volume III of The History of Middle-earth). During a magical "whetting spell," Beleg invokes several legendary weapons of the past. Among them is the glaive of Gaurin, described as a weapon whose shining stroke split the rocks of Rodrim's hall.

entities.name: High Fells of Rhudaur
entities.description:
The High Fells of Rhudaur was the location of the tombs made for the Nazgûl, created following their defeat at the hands of the Men of Arnor.

Described more as a prison of the dead than as a grave, the tombs were located north of the Trollshaws (which used to part of the lands of Rhudaur before its collapse); near the source of the river Hoarwell and south of the Coldfells.

The High Fells and its corresponding history were created for Peter Jackson's , and are thus non-canonical.

In , the tombs are first mentioned by Lady Galadriel during the meeting of the White Council in Rivendell as part of their discussion concerning the rediscovery of the Witch-king of Angmar's Morgul-blade by Radagast in the ruins of Dol Guldur. The tombs are revealed as the location where the Witch-king was buried following the fall of the realm of Angmar, entombed there by the men of the North. The tombs themselves are said to be so dark that they would never come to light. As noted by Elrond, powerful spells lie upon the tombs, which should have prevented the crypts from ever being opened. Saruman however, rules that there is not enough proof that the Morgul-blade actually originated from the Witch-king's grave, and dismisses it.

entities.name: Elven-brooches
entities.description:
Elven-brooches, also known as leaves of Lórien, were brooches given by Galadriel as gifts to the members of the Fellowship of the Ring (except for Gandalf, presumed at the time to be dead) at the end of their stay at Lothlórien. They appeared as the new-opened leaves of a beech-tree.

In , after the breaking of the Fellowship, Peregrin Took intentionally dropped his brooch while being carried by Uruk-hai as a signal to Aragorn, Legolas, and Gimli, who were tracking the captured hobbits, that they were on the correct trail. In Henneth Annûn, Frodo showed his leaf to Faramir as proof of his claim to his friendship to Boromir, as well as his time spent in Lothlórien.

In Peter Jackson's , according to Celeborn, all the surviving Fellowship were given brooches in the form of a green leaf veined with silver to clasp the elven-cloaks they were also given.

entities.name: Ogbar
entities.description:
Ogbar was an individual who owned a spear that might be related to Gaurin's glaive.

In the final centuries of the First Age, after Túrin had been captured by Orcs, his friend Beleg and the Nargothronder Gwindor rescued him from the enemy's camp while he was still chained and unconscious. Once they took him nearby, Beleg sought sharpen his sword to cut Túrin's chains, and whispered a whetting spell, and invoked many great objects of power, such as Ogbar's spear, which might be related to Gaurin's spear that was said to have once rived "the rocks of Rodrim's hall".

Ogbar is a Sindarin name with an untold meaning.

entities.name: Nordinbad
entities.description:
Nordinbad as it appears in War in the North ]]

Nordinbad is a location in the game The Lord of the Rings: War in the North. It is a Dwarven fortress hidden deep within the Grey Mountains, providing isolation and refuge for the Dwarves of Durin's Folk who have inhabited it since before the Dwarves fled the Grey Mountains. They lived around an underground lake known as Azan-zâram.

Gorin of the Longbeards was the Lord of Nordinbad.

Centuries before the War of the Ring, the great-great grandsire of Lord Gorin, discovered the caves in which dwelt the hidden lake that would be called Azan-zâram. He chose to lead some of his kin there and over the course of many years, they slowly built the hall that they would name, Nordinbad. Though Nordinbad was never wealthy in gold or jewels, the inhabitants considered it to be rich in beauty. So they took great care to enhance and preserve this beauty and to never defile it.

entities.name: Fire of Doom
entities.description:
The Fire of Doom, or simply the Fire, was the caldera and/or magma chamber inside Mount Doom. A boiling lake of magma deep inside the mountain that was named by a voice heard by Samwise Gamgee coming from a figure robed in white, but afterwards appeared to be Frodo Baggins.

On July 19, of 2022, Mark Fisher speculated on The Encyclopedia of Arda Sauron's ability to control the Fire of Doom may be due to a connection to the One Ring.

entities.name: Rodrim
entities.description:
Rodrim was an individual who owned a hall that was riven by Gaurin's glaive.

In the final centuries of the First Age, after Túrin had been captured by Orcs, his friend Beleg and the Nargothronder Gwindor rescued him from the enemy's camp while he was still chained and unconscious. Once they took him nearby, Beleg sought sharpen his sword to cut Túrin's chains, and whispered a whetting spell, and invoked many great objects of power, such as Gaurin's glaive, which was said to have once rived "the rocks of Rodrim's hall".

Rodrim is a Sindarin name with an untold meaning.

entities.name: The Southern Gate
entities.description:
The Southern Gate is the fourth level of video game.

Aragorn is making his way through the gate to Gondor. But before he can, the gate closes and from it an Uruk captain jumps down. After killing the Uruk captain, the player may kill battle the Uruks freely. After firing two catapults at any point, the player must go to the top of the gate and defeat another Uruk captain and a new enemy, the Mûmakil, and then open the gate for good. After leaving the gate, the player must kill the Uruk-hai before going through the gate to finish the level.

The player may choose any of these once The Crack of Doom is completed. Category:Non-canon locations Category:The Return of the King (video game) Levels
entities.short_description: The Southern Gate is the fourth level of video game.

entities.name: Galadriel's gifts
entities.description:
During the Quest of Mount Doom, Galadriel gave eight gifts to the remaining members of the Fellowship of the Ring (after the loss of Gandalf) soon before they departed from Lothlórien.

On February 16 in the year 3019 of the Third Age, Galadriel gave each member of the Fellowship of the Ring a gift to help them on their way. She gave Aragorn a magical Elven scabbard and the Elessar, a green gem set in a silver eagle shaped brooch, left for him by Arwen. To Boromir, she gave a solid belt of gold that was crafted in Lothlórien in the shape of linked golden leaves. To Legolas, she gave a bow of the Galadhrim with a quiver of arrows, crafted deep in Lothlórien and strung with elf-hair. Both Merry and Pippin received a silver belt with a gold, flower-shaped clasp. Samwise was given earth from Galadriel's garden, and a Mallorn seed - These were contained in a small box of grey wood with a silver G-rune on the lid. When Galadriel asked Gimli what he wanted of her, he modestly refused, but when pressed, he could think of nothing else he wanted but a single strand of her hair. She gave him three, as well as a blessing that his hands would ever flow with gold, though it would have no dominion over his mind. Galadriel then gave Frodo Baggins a small crystal vial in which was caught the light of Eärendil's star in the water of Galadriel's fountain. The phial emitted a brilliant light in darkness, so intense that dark creatures fear it.

After Gandalf saved Samwise Gamgee's and Frodo’s gifts, Samwise Gamgee used it to replant trees in the Shire after the Scouring of the Shire.
